sources.title: How Zach Yadegari built Cal AI to $1M+/month at 17 with influencer marketing
sources.originalTitle: The 17-Year-Old Who Built a $1.12M/Month Ai App | Zach Yadegari
sources.summary: Zach explains how he went from a school unblocked-games site to Cal AI, a bootstrapped calorie-tracking app doing over $1M/month. He lays out his playbook: validate virality before building, buy short-form influencer videos using RPM vs CPM math, hard paywall with a trial, then layer on paid ads using influencer creatives.

principles.text: Validate how an idea will go viral on social media before building it.
principles.quote: it's making sure that we know how we're going to blow it up if we have a product that we think this is a really cool product but there's nothing to tap into on social media no Niche no influencer to promote it it's going to be 10 times harder

principles.text: Influencer deals must be profitable: revenue per 1,000 views (RPM) must exceed cost per 1,000 views (CPM).
principles.quote: every dollar you pay per thousand views needs to be less than the amount of money you will make per thousand views

principles.text: Pay influencers upfront based on predicted views, and bundle several videos on retainer to bring the price down.
principles.quote: we'll do four videos with you we'll pay upfront all the money for them and that's usually one of the main tactics we do to actually get the price down a lot

principles.text: Make sponsored integrations seamless so they don't feel like ads.
principles.quote: We make the integration super super seamless where people don't even know it's an ad

principles.text: Outreach is a numbers game; most people quit after 100 DMs and never negotiate creatively.
principles.quote: people give up after dming 100 influencers you have to DM thousands

principles.text: Hard paywall utility apps with a free trial instead of going free with ads or a premium upgrade.
principles.quote: people shouldn't be scared to just hard pay wall and not let anyone use the app without paying upfront

sources.title: How Zach Yadegari scaled Cal AI to $50M ARR and sold it to MyFitnessPal at 18
sources.originalTitle: Zach Yadegari: Selling Cal Ai for millions at 18-years-old
sources.summary: Zach explains how Cal AI grew from influencer-only marketing (~$2M/month) to $5.7M/month by adding performance ads and a creator affiliate program. He covers attribution hacks, ad creative, co-founder roles, hiring, and the speed and self-belief mindset behind the exit.

principles.text: Once influencer audiences overlap and saturate, broaden to non-niche creators and add performance ads as a new growth channel.
principles.quote: all of the influencers in the fitness space, all the big ones at least, we'd pretty much worked with and a lot of these fitness influencers share the same audiences. So it was a smaller bang for the buck working with more fitness influencers.

principles.text: Use custom App Store product pages per ad channel to get clean attribution, then gross it up ~30% for people who search the app by name.
principles.quote: you can actually create custom product pages for apps on the App Store. And for each custom product page, you're able to see the amount of revenue that that page by itself generated.

principles.text: Keep ad campaign structure simple and let creative be the strategy; target with creative rather than audience settings.
principles.quote: You want to set up your campaign structures in a very simple way and creative is key. Creative is the whole strategy. You just set it up once and then it's all about the creative.

principles.text: Influencer videos with the app as a subtle cameo cap out in ads; videos dedicated to directly selling the app scaled spend from ~10-15K to ~40K a day.
principles.quote: Then once we started making actual videos where the whole the whole video is dedicated to, okay, this is an app I've been using recently where it lets me track my calories super easily throughout my day.

principles.text: Run an affiliate program where creators make ad-ready videos for a revenue share, instead of directing creative yourself.
principles.quote: we have an affiliate program that lets any creator make videos for us and then they just get a percentage of the revenue. And so we have some creators making a lot of money.

principles.text: Hiring real talent and setting vision matters more than founder hustle once you have product-market fit; speed is the core value.
principles.quote: As soon as we started investing in real talent that's when like the company just started growing on its own.

sources.title: How Zach Yadegari scaled Cal AI to $30M revenue and sold it to MyFitnessPal at 19
sources.originalTitle: Zach is 18 & made $50m from an app. Here's the brutal breakdown of how he did it (and you can too)
sources.summary: Zach explains how Cal AI grew from influencer marketing to performance ads and how he ran his first acquisition. He covers playing hard to get, warm intros, expected-value thinking, and how he validates app ideas by treating competitors as proof of demand.

principles.text: Influencer marketing got Cal AI to ~$2M/month; performance ads on Instagram, TikTok and Facebook unlocked the next stage.
principles.quote: influencer marketing is what started us and it took us really far. We got to about $2 million a month just from influencer marketing. The thing is after that we kind of plateaued a little bit.

principles.text: A big creator sponsorship can pay back through credibility that unlocks more deals, even if the direct return is unprofitable.
principles.quote: having the brand name Mr. be saying we were in a video, we were able to do way more deals afterwards. We had way more credibility with our brand

principles.text: When selling a company, get warm intros rather than cold outreach, since cold outreach loses leverage.
principles.quote: I was recommended that or I heard somewhere it's you lose leverage if you're just cold outreaching.

principles.text: In acquisition talks, play hard to get: show interest but signal you're going somewhere regardless.
principles.quote: you basically want to play hard to get kind of you don't want to you don't want to be too interested.

principles.text: Use expected value to weigh selling now versus keep going, instead of deciding on emotion.
principles.quote: EV is a good one. So, like gamblers obviously know this where it's like the percent chance of winning something and then the prize and you multiply them together.

principles.text: Skill at validating ideas matters more than generating them; an existing competitor is proof of demand, not a reason to quit.
principles.quote: I think the more important skill and the better skill is a framework to validate what is a good idea because you could come up with ideas all the time

sources.title: How Zach Yadegari grew Cal AI to $2M a month as a high schooler with influencers
sources.originalTitle: You’re One AI Idea Away From Changing Your Life
sources.summary: Zach explains how Cal AI (photo calorie tracker) hit about $20M ARR in 10 months, bootstrapped, through paid influencer marketing. He shares how he validates ideas with an AI wrapper, picks AI app ideas by working backwards from an "aha moment," and why he stayed focused on one app.

principles.text: Start as an AI wrapper to prove demand, then build the real product once it works.
principles.quote: it's true that we started as an AI rapper and I think that that's something all apps should do just like in Ecom it's very common to start as a drop shipper and drop ship a product and then once you find success actually manufacture it yourself

principles.text: Ignore feedback from family and friends; it's biased. Get real signal from influencers' audiences.
principles.quote: family and friends although we just disregarded anything from them because I always think it's biased

principles.text: Grow through paid influencer marketing; hire creators who know what goes viral and predict ROI.
principles.quote: we just pay the influencer that fits our Niche and then they're the professionals they know what goes viral as long as we can predict the RO Y

principles.text: Not all views are equal: judge a creator's comment section and community strength when deciding what to pay.
principles.quote: not all views are worth the same you have to analyze the comment section and see how strong their Community is

principles.text: Find ideas by working backwards from a marketable aha moment, then wrap a sticky app around it.
principles.quote: I look for an aha moment that I could capture within some sort of experience and then wrap a whole app around that

principles.text: Once a product is scaling, focus on it rather than spinning up side apps; improvements compound.
principles.quote: we realized pretty quickly that it made more sense to stay full-time on CI because the same time it would take to build another app and scale it to six figures Revenue we could have added an additional seven figures in Revenue to CI

sources.title: Zach Yadegari's blueprint for building and marketing an AI skin-scan app (Dr AI)
sources.originalTitle: Inside the Brain of a 17-Year-Old $1M/Month AI Founder
sources.summary: Zach walks through a full blueprint for a Cal AI-style utility app: design the UX around what an influencer will show on screen, reuse existing UI primitives, and prompt GPT carefully. He covers audience-first influencer research, RPM vs CPM deal math, and weekly subscription pricing tested via A/B experiments.

principles.text: Design the app around what an influencer will show; it must communicate its value in 2 seconds.
principles.quote: showing it on an influencer video when it when the phone is only on the screen for 2 seconds you need the viewer to understand what this app does and why they want to get it for themselves

principles.text: Find the one wow-factor feature influencers will demo, and put the app name on that screen.
principles.quote: with influencer videos you always want to think about what the biggest wow factor of the app will be what the specific feature that will wow the audience is and make them think I should get this

principles.text: Pick influencers by reading their comments to learn the real audience, not their stated niche.
principles.quote: it's always important to look at the audience of the influencer not at the actual influencer their Niche could be one thing but Their audience could be something completely different

principles.text: Pay creators upfront and make sure revenue per thousand views beats cost per thousand; assume a $5 RPM to start.
principles.quote: to ensure that your RPM is greater than your CPM which is the way to ensure post is profitable that you're making more per thousand views than your spending

principles.text: Don't strand users on a loading screen; send them home and show the loading state there.
principles.quote: I think it's much better to take the user straight back to the home screen and then have a loading here so it's it doesn't make them feel like they're forced to wait on an empty screen

principles.text: For infrequent-need utility apps, test weekly pricing, with and without free trials, and optimize for proceeds per download.
principles.quote: I AB test a bunch of things so what I'll usually do is I'll AB test $4 a week $7 a week I'll try variations of a free trial on both of those

sources.title: How Zach Yadegari grew Cal AI to $1.1M a month with influencer marketing and no paid ads
sources.originalTitle: How To Make $1.1M a Month With AI Apps (No Paid Ads) | Zach Yadegari
sources.summary: Zach Yadegari, 17, explains how Cal AI reached $1.1M monthly revenue through influencer Stories tests, organic creator videos and virtual assistants sending bulk DMs. He also covers onboarding and paywall tweaks, pricing tests, and why core growth levers should not be outsourced.

principles.text: Test influencers cheaply through Stories before paying for full videos, so you can iterate faster across creators and niches.
principles.quote: جعلنا المؤثرين الأوائل ينشرون عبر قصصهم (ستوريز)، وليس كمقطع فيديو كامل. وهذا سمح لنا بالتجربة بشكل أسرع بين مختلف المؤثرين والمجالات، لأن قصص ستوري أرخص

principles.text: Build the product around a visual wow moment; creators show it naturally while the app name appears on screen.
principles.quote: نحن نضع اسم" كالي " بشكل بارز في الصفحة الرئيسية في الأعلى.

principles.text: In cold DMs, the goal is getting the creator to open and reply: keep it short, human and respectful of their time.
principles.quote: أهم شيء في النظام بأكمله هو جعل المؤثر يفتح الرسالة فعلياً وإغرائه بالرد.

principles.text: Don't outsource a core growth lever; your edge comes from owning it yourself.
principles.quote: لا أعتقد أن الاستعانة بمصادر خارجية لإدارة عامل أساسي أمر ذكي لاستمرار العمل أو نموه على الإطلاق.

principles.text: Lengthening onboarding with animations raised conversion, because users who invest time want to try the app.
principles.quote: مجرد إضافة رسوم متحركة بين الشاشات، والتي ربما ضاعفت طول مسار التهيئة، أدى إلى زيادة معدل التحويل في النهاية بنسبة 10%.

principles.text: Choose pricing by what you optimize: he kept the lower price to retain users who spread the app by word of mouth.
principles.quote: وقررنا أن الحفاظ على هذه الـ 30% أفضل حالياً لأنهم سينشرون التطبيق عبر الكلام الشفهي

sources.title: How Zach Yadegari built Cal AI to $1M/month at 17: speed, influencer systems, bootstrapping
sources.originalTitle: Meet The 17-Year-Old Making $1M/Month With AI
sources.summary: Zach Yadegari recounts selling his unblocked-games site for ~$100K, then building Cal AI to $1M/month in revenue with no outside capital. He explains his speed-first mindset, a scalable influencer marketing system built on CPM vs RPM math, fast validation, and why distribution is the real bottleneck for consumer apps.

principles.text: Speed is the core value: ship a first version in days, not months, because consumer markets punish slowness.
principles.quote: I think moving quickly I mean if I hadn't moved fast I wouldn't have accomplished anything that I've done today.

principles.text: Distribution, not product, is the consumer bottleneck; developers are easy to find but distributing the app is hard.
principles.quote: distribution 100% is where the advantage lies within everything that I'm doing within my companies

principles.text: Scale influencer marketing by starting scrappy with heavy outreach; credibility and referrals then compound into a network effect.
principles.quote: you reply to 100 influencers maybe if you get lucky one will reply to you after you do it long enough you'll start building up your initial base of influencers and this will compound

principles.text: Keep influencers on retainer with deals priced so the revenue per thousand views exceeds the CPM you pay.
principles.quote: you need to ensure that your RPM the revenue you generate from those same thousand views exceeds the CPM

principles.text: Validate ideas fast and cheap; don't spend a year building before launching. Get a rough prototype out and collect feedback or pre-payment.
principles.quote: it doesn't need to be good by any means the first prototype for CI we developed in 3 weeks launched it got feedback

principles.text: Raising capital can remove urgency; consumer apps that work usually show it quickly, so you need little money to test feasibility.
principles.quote: if it's no longer your money that you're dealing with then failure doesn't seem as disastrous

sources.title: How Zach Yadegari built Cal AI to $2M/month at 17: aha-feature apps, influencer ROI, and yearly pricing
sources.originalTitle: App Expert: How to Build Viral Apps in 30 Days, Make Millions at 17, and Retire Before College
sources.summary: Zach lays out his repeatable playbook for viral consumer apps: find one captivating "aha" feature, ship an MVP in a month, test with the single ideal influencer, and scale only when influencer ROI is profitable. He also covers pricing tests, co-founder equity, copycats, and his build-fast, ship-many mindset.

principles.text: Start marketing-first: find one eye-catching 'aha' feature, then build the whole product around it.
principles.quote: I always like to think about things from a marketing first perspective. I like to find an idea that is eye-catching, that is captivating, that is useful, and then build a full product around it.

principles.text: Keep the MVP to the main feature plus the minimum around it, and ship it within a month.
principles.quote: getting an MVP out, which I don't like to spend more than a month on, which should basically be that main feature, and then the minimum amount of components around that to still give a good user experience.

principles.text: Validate with the one ideal influencer in the niche; if it fails with them, rework or scrap the idea.
principles.quote: if that's your ideal influencer for the product and it doesn't work with them, it's not going to work with anyone.

principles.text: Judge influencers by views and predicted ROI, not followers; the hard part is estimating ROI before paying.
principles.quote: Followers don't matter at all. It's only the views they get.

principles.text: Let creators make native content and sneak the product in; don't dictate the creative.
principles.quote: We just want them to plug in our product into the content that already works really well for them and almost sneak it in there.

principles.text: A/B test paywalls and prices; a cheaper yearly plan with a free trial beat a higher price on revenue per download.
principles.quote: because more people would subscribe to the 30 a year, we would make more money on average per download.

sources.title: Zach Yadegari on AI apps: validate proven ideas, add a viral hook, and plan life around curiosity
sources.originalTitle: Brain Chips are Coming: 18 Year Old Tech Founder - Zach Yadegari
sources.summary: Wide-ranging first episode of the Blake Anderson podcast. Zach explains why cheap public AI APIs let small teams beat funded incumbents, shares his app-store playbook for turning $5,000 into $100,000, and describes how he picks long-term goals by following curiosity instead of one fixed purpose. Much of the talk drifts into philosophy, brain chips and AI's social impact.

principles.text: Cheap public AI APIs let small teams build what was once impossible and outrun funded incumbents.
principles.quote: since all these APIs are publicly available, anyone for very cheap cost, just a few cents for thousands of AI calls can do anything.

principles.text: Look at any product that lacks AI and ask where AI would help; monotonous tasks are the opening.
principles.quote: I think that you can look at almost any industry, any product right now that doesn't use AI and find ways that AI would be useful.

principles.text: Use a simple filter for AI opportunity: anything monotonous gets replaced.
principles.quote: The framework that I like to look at is anything that's monotonous can be and will be replaced.

principles.text: Start from validated demand: find top or rising apps that are poorly built or lack AI, then rebuild with a stronger viral hook.
principles.quote: find apps that are ranking the highest or find new apps that are up and coming ones that ideally don't use AI or ones that are just built poorly. They clearly have virality to them.

principles.text: The idea is already validated, so your edge is a hook you can feature in short-form promo videos, then scale with influencers.
principles.quote: It's already validated. I would create a hook within it.

principles.text: Aim at things you want to have done by the end of life, then sequence them, instead of optimizing one fixed purpose.
principles.quote: what do I want to have done by the time I'm maybe 80 and on a deathbed.

sources.title: How a 14-year-old built totally science, a 300K-visitor unblocked games site, and what he learned
sources.originalTitle: Zach Yadegari - 16-year-old founder, CEO, and developer
sources.summary: Zach Yadegari explains how he built an unblocked games hub in 8th grade, grew it through TikTok and school-to-school word of mouth, and monetized it with AdSense. He covers scaling pains, small-team structure, and his views on college and next projects.

principles.text: Build the thing you see people already doing badly: consolidate scattered behavior into one hub.
principles.quote: I saw a lot of people had different tabs open with different games on each Tab and different websites with each game and so I decided it would be much better if there was one website that was a hub for all of these games

principles.text: Ship a simple v1 fast; improve it only once real traffic shows it matters.
principles.quote: the original site took me probably just a few days it was very simple it was just a basic layout with games on it nothing fancy at all

principles.text: Ride trending demand: add what's trending, then post a TikTok about it to spark a viral spike.
principles.quote: Retro Bowl is a game that it's like a little football pixel game on phones but there's also versions on computers and on Tik Tok it was trending people trying to play it at school

principles.text: Seed one user per school from organic TikTok, then let peer-to-peer spread do the rest; put the brand name on screen so others see it.
principles.quote: getting an original just one like person in every school just from the organic Tik Tok videos and then from there it spreads organically to everyone else in the district

principles.text: Mine comments for demand and reply with videos announcing the requested feature or game.
principles.quote: another way we try to Market is by looking at the comments finding a game and then replying to that comment with a video saying we just added this game

principles.text: Keep the team tiny with revenue share instead of hiring when the product doesn't need more hands.
principles.quote: we have a a revenue share between us okay that's how our relationship is that's awesome

sources.title: How Zach Yadegari went from a school unblocked-games site to Cal AI and viral iOS apps
sources.originalTitle: This 17-Year-Old is Leading AI App Development -- From School Games to Viral Apps!
sources.summary: Zach tells how he grew Totally Science to 5M users via classroom TikTok videos, sold it on Flippa, then moved to iOS apps. He covers revamping Grind Clock into a subscription app, launching Cal AI with organic TikTok, why he avoids raising capital, and building in-house tools.

principles.text: Spot a fragmented behavior and consolidate it into one hub; Totally Science combined scattered game sites.
principles.quote: I identified the opportunity to combine all of these games on different websites under one website which acted as a hub and that was totally science

principles.text: Market via self-made social content showing the product in its real context, not paid ads.
principles.quote: I created content myself just recording myself in class playing on the website and I attained a few million views from the videos I posted

principles.text: Revisit apps that still get organic downloads; revamp them and switch to subscriptions.
principles.quote: we saw clearly people liked the app we could say that was probably attributed partially to the Tik Tok video still getting some views

principles.text: Not raising capital forces profitability and urgency from day one.
principles.quote: not having Capital raised puts a fire under you that forces is you to make it work and one it needs to be profitable from the start

principles.text: Take incumbent apps' necessary features and make them easier with AI; prove accuracy with a test bench.
principles.quote: first we took all the features that were necessary and we made them easier with AI now we're going to take all the features that are useful and make those easier with AI as well

principles.text: Build in-house testing tools to move fast and reuse them across future apps, like app studios do.
principles.quote: we will be able to repurpose them with future apps so we will be able to just easily put our foot in the door in a new industry

sources.title: How Cal AI's Zach Yadegari grew with influencers and kept the momentum
sources.originalTitle: Going Viral Is the Easy Part: Cal AI's Zach Yadegari on Keeping the Momentum | Disrupt 2026
sources.summary: Zach Yadegari explains how Cal AI scaled through paid influencer posts, then added paid ads, and why he treats retention as a product problem. He also covers lessons from his failed apps, such as charging users from day one, and how he plans to apply them to Persona.

principles.text: Test distribution cheaply: one paid influencer story with a fitting audience proved the channel before scaling it.
principles.quote: حصلنا على أول عملائنا على الإطلاق من خلال أحد المؤثرين. وجدنا شخصاً كان يوثق رحلته في إنقاص الوزن.

principles.text: Choose influencers for engaged, loyal communities rather than raw views, because not every view is worth the same.
principles.quote: كان أهم شيء بالنسبة لنا هو العثور على مؤثرين لديهم مجتمعات مترابطة وجمهور متفاعل. لأن الناس يمكنهم الحصول على مشاهدات، لكن ليست كل مشاهدة لها نفس القيمة.

principles.text: Negotiate creator deals by asking for more deliverables at the same price, which lowers your cost per video.
principles.quote: سندفع لك هذا المبلغ، لكن عليك تقديم أربعة فيديوهات لنا بدلاً من ذلك

principles.text: Organic viral content does not transfer to paid ads. Make creative built specifically for paid channels.
principles.quote: أدركنا أننا نحتاج إلى فهم أن المحتوى الذي ينجح مع الخوارزميات بشكل عضوي يختلف كثيراً عما يؤدي أداءً جيداً في الإعلانات الممولة.

principles.text: Treat retention as a product problem: improving the product (e.g. scan accuracy) improves retention.
principles.quote: نظرنا إلى الاحتفاظ بالمستخدمين باعتباره مشكلة تتعلق بالمنتج، حيث أن تحسين المنتج سيؤدي طبيعياً إلى تحسين الاحتفاظ بهم.

principles.text: Charge for the app instead of relying on in-app ads. Users will pay for subscriptions, and ads earn little.
principles.quote: لكننا تعلمنا بعد القيام بذلك أن، أولاً، الإعلانات داخل التطبيقات لا تجني الكثير من الإيرادات، وثانياً، أن الناس سيدفعون بالفعل مقابل استخدام التطبيقات.

sources.title: How to start a business: Zach Yadegari's fundamentals from building Cal AI
sources.originalTitle: How to start a business
sources.summary: Zach Yadegari (Cal AI founder, 19) lays out the basics of building a profitable business: product, selling, LTV vs CAC, scalability, delegating to employees with aligned incentives, and a bias toward speed. He also covers hiring, pricing via A/B testing, idea generation, co-founders and the mindset needed to absorb constant setbacks.

principles.text: A business is a product plus selling it; to be profitable, LTV must exceed CAC plus cost of goods.
principles.quote: your LTV needs to be greater than the CAC plus the cost of the good.

principles.text: Make both the product and the marketing channel scalable, not just profitable.
principles.quote: you want to make sure that your product is scalable. It's profitable. That's good, but it needs to be scalable.

principles.text: Hire people smarter than you with initiative, and use interviews to scare off non-grinders.
principles.quote: You also always want to hire people smarter than you.

principles.text: Align incentives with equity or KPI-tied bonuses so employees care; you can't really overpay great talent.
principles.quote: I would very strongly recommend that you should have something that aligns incentives. If it's not bonuses, then equity.

principles.text: Move fast with a bias toward action; ideas are worthless without execution.
principles.quote: Execution is everything. Ideas are worthless.

principles.text: Only traffic, conversion rate and retention/LTV matter; double down on what already works and A/B test everything.
principles.quote: If they double down on that, which now they are, it's like, okay, let's focus on paid ads.

sources.title: How Zach Yadegari launched Flow Alarm: subscription upsell, LTV-based CAC, and cash discipline
sources.originalTitle: How I'm Building a Billion Dollar Company (Episode 1)
sources.summary: Episode 1 of Zach's open-source journey building Flow, a physical alarm-clock dock. He covers picking a big-TAM product, pre-selling during a manufacturing delay, and fixing unit economics with a subscription attach at checkout. The key lesson: spend up to full LTV on acquisition while testing pricing and verifying data.

principles.text: Pick products with huge TAM that everyone uses daily, especially where incumbents aren't innovating.
principles.quote: The things with the biggest TAMs are really the things that everyone uses on a [music] day-to-day basis. And some of the biggest companies are just companies that aren't innovating on [music] some of the technologies people use every day.

principles.text: Pre-sell with scarcity and honest ship delays instead of waiting on slow manufacturing.
principles.quote: We put a pre-sale, but we did [music] it in a very unique way. Made it feel like there was a lot of scarcity, but we made it clear like your order is not going to ship for a while, but get it now.

principles.text: Keep media buying simple: master the fundamentals and turn off Meta's extra automations.
principles.quote: turning off all the extra [ __ ] that Metatries to turn on for you and just keeping it [music] simple stupid.

principles.text: Raise LTV with a subscription attached to the product; that's what unlocks scaling spend.
principles.quote: So, what's going to take us to the millions is increasing the LTV, which will mostly come from the subscriptions.

principles.text: When revenue recurs, spend up to full LTV on acquisition and profit on renewals, not day one.
principles.quote: A smart business person would recognize that this $41 is a recurring subscription. the smart business person would spend $41.

principles.text: Don't trust a single dashboard; trace anomalies to the root and A/B test price points.
principles.quote: We use triple whale and I realize all of this data is [ __ ] inaccurate.

sources.title: Building Flow: killing a profitable but deceptive subscription while chasing $100M
sources.originalTitle: How I'm Building a Billion Dollar Company (Episode 2)
sources.summary: Episode 2 of Zach's Flow alarm clock build log. He shows launch pain from a subscription upsell, funnel and price A/B tests, and what he learned from advisors. He ends by dropping a profitable subscription model because customers didn't realize they were being subscribed.

principles.text: Don't scale profit built on customers not realizing they're subscribed; protect brand even at a short-term loss.
principles.quote: I don't like that it's deceptive that people are being subscribed without realizing it. So, we're going to the one-time purchase, no subscription model.

principles.text: A bad first-product experience closes the door on future products, so protect the customer experience.
principles.quote: We want to have a bunch of different products for Flow in the future. And if customers have a bad experience with the first one, they're not going to get any in the future.

principles.text: Ship an imperfect v1, then prioritize support and refunds to fix it over time.

sources.title: How Zach Yadegari built Cal AI to $1.4M/month at 18: AI photo calorie tracking and influencer marketing
sources.originalTitle: How I Built A $1.4 Million/Month AI App At Age 18
sources.summary: Zach Yadegari explains how he spotted a pain point in calorie tracking apps, used AI to remove the friction, and went all-in with his co-founders. He covers influencer marketing as Cal AI's core growth engine, reinvesting profits, and the cash-flow lag from Apple's payout schedule.

principles.text: Build around the friction that made you quit a competitor's product; AI removes the manual work.
principles.quote: the app required me to weigh my food on a scale, type in everything I was eating. It was unsustainable for my lifestyle.

principles.text: When early response to a launch is strongly positive, go all-in and commit full time.
principles.quote: The response immediately was very positive. That's when we knew we had something good on our hands and we decided to go allin.

principles.text: Influencer marketing is the special sauce, and most of the spend goes there.
principles.quote: Our special sauce at Cali, what we really do, right, is influencer marketing. And that's where a far majority of our spending goes to.

principles.text: Concentrated time with the team, first hires and a good rhythm can be the turning point.
principles.quote: we moved to San Francisco for the month of July. We stayed there for a month, lived in a hacker house, basically slept in the office

principles.text: Reinvest most revenue into the product and growth; pay dividends only from leftover cash.
principles.quote: We reinvest most of the money back into the app from Cali, but whenever there's enough cash left over, we will pay out dividends to ourselves.

principles.text: App store payout delays mean fast scaling can drain cash even when profitable; plan for the lag.
principles.quote: we were scaling faster than Apple was paying us, which meant that for months we were putting money in and weren't seeing a proportional amount of money out.

sources.title: App Mafia: how Zach Yadegari and co-founders scale consumer apps with influencers, controversy and speed
sources.originalTitle: #40 - WTF is App Mafia - 18/yo earning $45M/yr building apps
sources.summary: Zach and the App Mafia crew (Cal AI, Quitter, Umax) explain how they scale hard-paywalled consumer apps: direct-response influencer marketing, occasional big mindshare bets like a $500K MrBeast sponsorship, controversy for reach, a tiny critical path, speed and bootstrapped risk-taking.

principles.text: Run marketing as direct response: price each influencer post against expected return, and scale only what is profitable.
principles.quote: pretty much most of our strategy comes down to direct response. It's not a lot of the whole brand awareness game. It's mostly, okay, we know we're paying this much for an influencer to post and we're going to get this much back

principles.text: Take occasional big mindshare bets (e.g. MrBeast) when second-order effects like trust, hiring and word of mouth justify it.
principles.quote: it's Mr. Beast, we know that there will be all of these second degree effects where working with him makes us more trustworthy with other brands.

principles.text: Climb up the influencer ladder gradually; pay for bigger names as revenue grows, and take bets that are survivable.
principles.quote: we have scaled up Cali almost only through influencers. Only recently are we starting to run paid ads like Facebook pay-per-click ads. And so we've just been working our way up to more and more famous influencers

principles.text: Focus 80% of time on the few metrics that matter in a hard-paywall app: downloads, conversion, retention; let small fires burn.
principles.quote: there are only really three things like Cali hard paywalled apps that truly matter. It's one getting people to download, two is converting the downloads and then three is getting them to stay.

principles.text: Ship fast and imperfect early; speed builds momentum and intuition, and killing a failed launch video quickly beats perfectionism.
principles.quote: the more decisions you make the the more data you And the stronger your intuition grows over time. If you do nothing, your intuition and and your your mental models are never going to form

principles.text: Controversy and social reach are a hiring and distribution advantage; avoiding risk out of ego limits influence.
principles.quote: The more algorithmic reach and distribution that you have, the higher quality talent that you can attract.

principles.text: Judge influencer sponsorships by long-term credibility, not just direct return; big-name association unlocks later deals.

principles.text: Use expected value (probability times prize, including the chance of collapse) to decide whether to sell versus keep going.
principles.quote: the percent chance of winning something and then the prize and you multiply them together.

principles.text: Favor ideas that are highly marketable and viral, in problems you've personally experienced or whose users you know.

sources.title: Zach Yadegari on self-belief, skill stacking, and how he sold his app company
sources.originalTitle: Zach Yadegari on Self Belief
sources.summary: Zach Yadegari explains how self-belief and "when, not if" language pushed him toward a teenage revenue goal, and why learning the 20% that matters lets you hire and manage smarter people. He also walks through selling his app company: a lowball first round, a mindset reset, warm intros, and leaning on founders who had sold before.

principles.text: Learn the 20% that delivers 80% of results so you can hire people smarter than you and manage them.
principles.quote: Learn the 20% that gets you the 80% of results. And that's what's necessary to actually hire someone that's smarter than you and being able to manage the team.

principles.text: Self-belief gets you past imagined prerequisites like degrees or classes; assume you can do it now.
principles.quote: I think self-belief has gotten me so far because it's helped me get over so many part points of life where I could have just said like ah like if no one like I have to go to college before I'm able to do this.

principles.text: Shift your language from "if" to "when" even while holding doubts.
principles.quote: I think I've been always conscious about like shifting my language to a when, not an if. Even though I of course I had doubts.

principles.text: Build products from a demand signal you see in the wild, like comments asking for something that doesn't exist.
principles.quote: everyone in the comments was like, "This got me so pumped up. I want to make this my alarm clock. How can I do that?" And there was no way to really easily do that.

principles.text: When selling a company, run a sales cycle: list target buyers and use warm intros to keep leverage.
principles.quote: I made a list of the 10 companies that I felt were made the most sense.

principles.text: In acquisition talks, play hard to get, and lean on founders who have sold before for advice.
principles.quote: What helped me the most was that I had a friend. I actually had a couple people that have been through acquisitions who were I was constantly getting on the phone with them and they were giving me advice throughout the whole process.

sources.title: Cal AI's growth bottleneck: fixing the "it's not accurate" narrative
sources.originalTitle: The biggest bottleneck for our growth
sources.summary: Zach reflects after Cal AI's best month (over $3M in May), explaining that the biggest growth bottleneck is public skepticism about accuracy. He lays out how he plans to counter it with influencer scripts, honest messaging and educating users on features beyond the viral scan, and what he would do differently on future projects.

principles.text: Find your biggest growth bottleneck by reading what people actually say about you, then make fixing it the main priority.
principles.quote: I'm analyzing all of our social media posts that have went out recently, and I'm realizing that I think the biggest bottleneck for our growth is really the fact that so many people still don't think Cali is accurate.

principles.text: Address trust and credibility objections from the start of scaling, before critics define the narrative.
principles.quote: I think from earlier on we should have handled this issue because now it's like kind of out of hand and it's going to be a big uphill battle.

principles.text: Viral content often shows only one feature; educate users on the rest of the product.
principles.quote: all of our marketing material really just shows the scanning feature because that's what goes viral. But so so most people don't know we have the database and barcode. So that's what we're trying to start educating users on.

principles.text: Be honest about product limits in messaging to build credibility against skepticism.
principles.quote: Cali does not have X-ray vision. can only track what it sees. It won't know how much oil you're using, so it will estimate the typical portion. And the scanner is not always 100% accurate. It's closer to 90%.

principles.text: Test a short message first, assess how people take it, then double down with longer content.
principles.quote: I think I'm going to start with this. assess how people take it and then double down.

principles.text: Sometimes you must take a step back to move two steps forward; chip away at a brick wall until you break through.
principles.quote: it kind of feels like we're taking a step back right now to do this, but it's in order to take two steps forward, which is sometimes necessary is what I've learned.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Zach explains how he went from a school unblocked-games site to Cal AI, a bootstrapped calorie-tracking app doing over $1M/month. He lays out his playbook: validate virality before building, buy short-form influencer videos using RPM vs CPM math, hard paywall with a trial, then layer on paid ads using influencer creatives.

chunks.heading: How Zach built Cal AI to $1M+/month at 17: product and idea selection
chunks.text:
Zach builds mobile consumer apps. Cal AI is an app where you take a picture of your food and it returns calories, carbs, protein and fat. He and his friend Henry (both in high school) started building apps about a year before this interview. Their first app, Grindclock (a motivational speaker like David Goggins screaming you out of bed), got 20,000 downloads in its first couple of weeks but they could not sustain the growth. Zach had been cold-messaging founders on X, including Blake Anderson (founder of two apps, Umax and RizzGPT, with a few million downloads combined). They worked out a partnership where Blake helps with high-level growth strategy as a co-founder while Zach and Henry run day-to-day operations. Cal AI has four co-founders (Zach 17, Henry 17, Blake 23, Jake 28) plus eight team members.

- **Idea source:** Existing calorie trackers like My Fitness Pal were outdated and convoluted. Zach wanted to bulk up and quit tracking after 3 days because it was so annoying. ChatGPT-era vision AI made a much simpler tracker possible.
- **Simplicity as positioning:** Cal AI sticks to calories, carbs, protein and fat. It skips sleep, hydration and other features. "We pride ourselves with how simple we are."
- **Validate distribution before building:** He validates ideas by making sure he knows how the product will blow up on social media. If there is "nothing to tap into" (no niche, no influencer to promote it), growth is "10 times harder." For Cal AI there were hundreds of health and fitness influencers whose audiences would love it, so "we just needed to build it and show it to them."
- **Inherent virality:** He only builds apps with built-in virality. Cal AI's core action (snap food, see calories) is instantly understandable, and the app name is shown at the top of the screen so viewers discover it. He says the idea is not genius: "we came in the Market at the right time" once the ChatGPT technology made it possible, and "we just moved quickly."
- **Build ideas you are the user of:** The best ideas come from a problem you or people around you have. If you are your ideal user "you'll know exactly what to build."
- **Results:** Launched about 6 months before the interview. Went from a May goal of $50K/month by end of summer to about $600K/month by then, and he shows App Store Connect at $1.14M for the month. Margins are about 50%, fully bootstrapped, profitable.
- **AI accuracy:** Version one was a single ChatGPT prompt, about 80% accurate (he equates this to the FDA's allowed margin of error on food labels). They then built a multi-prompt pipeline that gets more specific by food type and reaches about 90% on average.
- **User expectations lesson:** Consumers expected "x-ray vision" (for example seeing steak under rice in a Chipotle bowl). He says to lower your baseline assumption of user intelligence and make the experience "foolproof." Cal AI added a guide on the first scan showing how to scan for best accuracy.
- **Tech stack:** Swift natively (earlier apps used Flutter and React Native, which felt "janky"), Firebase Cloud Functions for the backend, Mixpanel for analytics, Slack for the team. They test extensively before updates.

chunks.heading: Influencer marketing system: finding, pricing and negotiating
chunks.text:
Influencer marketing is Cal AI's main channel (roughly 150 influencers posting regularly at the time). Zach says this is the first time he has publicly shared the full system.

- **Finding influencers:** Create a new TikTok account and only engage with health and fitness videos so the For You page feeds only creators in the niche. Copy the accounts into a Google Sheet with average views and followers. He did this himself at first; now virtual assistants do it.
- **Outreach volume:** About 1 in 100 influencers reply to DMs, and after 500 DMs you might get two decent ones. "People give up after DMing 100 influencers. You have to DM thousands." Prefer DMs over email, because email usually reaches managers, whose rates are higher and who are harder to negotiate with.
- **Core math (RPM vs CPM):** You pay the influencer enough that what you spend per thousand views (CPM) is below what you earn per thousand views (RPM). Predict views from their last ~10 videos and past brand deals, then pay a flat upfront fee. Example: 50,000 average views at a $2 CPM is about $100 per video.
- **Starting assumption:** When testing a new niche he starts at a $5 RPM (revenue per 1,000 views) and then watches trends. A niche brands have not tapped (he cites looksmaxxing) allows lower CPMs and a much higher RPM. For Cal AI, he targets roughly a $2-$3 CPM against that $5 RPM.
- **Engagement-adjusted pay:** Not all views are equal. Pay a lower rate for poor engagement and more for strong engagement.
- **Reading engagement:** Check the comment section. Good signs are people replying to each other, personal "you inspired me" comments, and top comments with 100+ likes. Red flags: comment bots, the same accounts on every video, or commenters who are all influencers (look for story rings on every profile), which signals a comment-for-comment pod.
- **Bundle and prepay for retainers:** Small creators often ask for far more than their views justify (for example $1,000 for a video averaging 50K views). Zach offers four videos paid upfront, which lowers the price and creates a monthly recurring retainer.
- **Negotiation framing:** "If they say I want $4,000 for one video, what they really mean is I want $4,000, I don't care how many videos I have to post." So give them the money but extend the number of videos, or use a "minimum view clause" (they must guarantee a view count or keep posting). Creators are "a dime a dozen" - for each one you can find 12 with the same views and engagement.
- **Pay-per-view deals:** Only work with smaller creators. Big ones will not agree.
- **Pay range:** He pays influencers from $100 a month up to $100,000 every two months for the largest one. Payment is by PayPal or bank transfer.
- **Content brief:** A simple one-pager with examples of past videos that worked, what the app does, things they can say and other ideas. Creators are professionals, so he lets them shoot it their way.

chunks.heading: Native-feeling integrations, comment control and repurposing
chunks.text:
- **Seamless integrations, no hard sell:** A lot of brands get this wrong with scripted reads like "this video is sponsored by X." Cal AI wants "what I eat in a day" or day-in-the-life videos where the influencer simply uses the app, often without ever saying the name. "People don't even know it's an ad." Zach tells creators to show the product in the first 15 seconds.
- **Let the product do the pitch:** Because scanning food is so novel, viewers see the app name on screen and ask what it is.
- **Control the comments:** Cal AI plants a comment in every video and has the creator pin it, replies to everyone who asks about the app, and makes sure everyone knows it is their app. He calls controlling the comment section "a big part of the strategy."
- **Repurposing content:** Cal AI owns the influencer videos and reposts every one on its own Instagram account (about 40,000 followers), getting tens of millions of views a month in addition to creator reach. The same video can be reposted after a few months because it reaches new viewers. TikTok flags duplicate videos, so the repost approach only works on Instagram. Early on, when you have no followers, DM influencers from a personal verified account, because response rates are much lower from an empty brand account. Once the brand account had tens of thousands of followers, replies improved.
- **Org setup for outreach:** Virtual assistants find influencers and do outreach, and a social media manager gets on calls and closes deals. Everyone logs in to the same brand account.

chunks.heading: Attribution and the viral.tech influencer platform
chunks.text:
- **Attribution problem:** Link-in-bio tracking does not work because viewers go straight to Google or the App Store after hearing about the app.
- **How he attributes:** Correlate the timing of an influencer post and its views with the download and revenue curves in App Store Connect over the same period. At scale, isolate which specific videos correlated most closely with downloads.
- **Planned product:** Zach says Cal AI's internal tools will launch publicly in early December as viral.tech (the transcript renders it "viral. te"). Pitch: a go-to-market strategy generator (who to target, what niche, how inherently viral your app is, content ideas), a CRM to track outreach status and active influencers, a posting schedule, post and view tracking, and attribution that overlays views on downloads.
- **Why he is doing it:** He believes influencer marketing will become ubiquitous and people are already reverse engineering Cal AI's strategy. If he brings it to market first and builds the platform everyone uses, he captures more upside than hoping no one competes.

chunks.heading: Pricing, paywall and onboarding psychology
chunks.text:
- **Pricing:** Cal AI is premium only, with $10 a month or $30 a year and a 3-day free trial. Most people choose yearly. There is no free tier. They had not yet measured retention because the app was under a year old.
- **Hard paywall lesson:** With Grindclock the premium upgrade was optional (ads plus a premium tier). After switching to a hard paywall they saw more revenue despite fewer downloads. Once people are used to something being free, "they don't want to pay." For a utility app that provides real value, "people shouldn't be scared to just hard paywall."
- **Onboarding questions raise conversion:** Onboarding asks weight, target weight, height and goals and why. An A/B test showed some questions have no functional purpose in calculating the plan, but asking them still raised conversion. His reasoning: each question ("why are you doing this?") makes users reflect on why they need the product, and the effort invested creates commitment, so by the time they see the paywall they are likelier to take the trial.
- **Fast time to value:** After onboarding users are dropped straight into scanning food. The app saves every meal and shows grams eaten versus grams left for the day. It does not recommend meals.

chunks.heading: Paid ads, Apple Search Ads and scaling
chunks.text:
- **Paid ads started ~2 months before the interview:** About $7,000 a day on Meta (Facebook and Instagram) and TikTok, profitable every day. He says paid ads are about 90% creative, and influencer content gives Cal AI a huge supply of creatives to test.
- **Sequencing:** Influencer marketing is more profitable in the short term and easier to get started, so use it first. His suggested order: build the product, reach out to ~100 creators, get ~2 to post, grow to ~20-30 influencers and ~100 pieces of content, then cycle into paid ads with the money generated. Paid ads should help scale further over the long term.
- **Apple Search Ads as a product test:** Running ads on a competitor's brand keyword in the App Store works as a validation signal. If your ad is profitable on their search term, that is usually a sign your product is better than theirs. If it is not, you are likely the worse product. He says this is not one-for-one but is a useful read.
- **Other ideas:** Considering TV ads. SEO is weak so far because the app is only six months old.
- **Scaling internally to scale externally:** At each stage he asks what has to change internally to hit the next milestone. After $100K/month they added developers, a full-time designer, more marketing help and more virtual assistants for outreach.
- **Distribution channels:** He notes the difference between scaling from $10M to $100M a month is mostly how many distribution channels you can competently master. Founders get held back at $50K-$100K a month because they do not scale their internal operations.
- **Cash flow:** Apple pays about two months later, so Cal AI continuously reinvests earnings from two months prior into current marketing. Founders had not yet paid themselves, expecting to within a month or two.
- **Competition and goals:** Competitors copy Cal AI after every tweet about its success. Cal AI usually ranks around number 10 in the App Store, behind long-established apps. His goal is to beat My Fitness Pal (he cites about $100M a year, stagnated) and then sell, possibly to My Fitness Pal.

chunks.heading: App studio strategy and mindset
chunks.text:
- **Why an app studio:** They have a network of health and fitness influencers, so new apps in the health and fitness category can be plugged into the same creators and deal structure. He says combining two apps in one deal with an influencer, paying more, gives more leverage to lower CPM.
- **Delegation:** Other apps are built by other developers with little of his time. Cal AI may deserve a double-down after seeing more potential than expected.
- **AI as a growth lever:** AI lets existing app categories be made more viral by attaching AI to a feature that is "a little bit cooler," which makes a social-friendly demo and can turn into a business.
- **Seasonal viral loop idea:** For Thanksgiving, he planned to make the app free for a day with a themed food scan and prompt users to post it to their stories (for example a "how festive is your dinner" angle), noting it might fail.
- **Role and mindset:** He moved from programmer to marketer to CEO focused on product and delegation. He says it helps to understand the technology deeply even if you are not the one programming.
- **Programming's future:** Programmers will need better product sense, knowing why a feature or button placement is right rather than just how to implement it.
- **Early history:** His unblocked games site (totally science dot com, categorized as an educational site) made about $660,000 a year and sold for $100,000 when he was 16 via Flippa. He grew it to 5 million users with TikTok videos recorded in class and asked viewers to comment which games to add next, which fed a reply-to-comment video series. He sold deliberately after meeting a 25-year-old founder whose high-school app had stalled, deciding to "burn the boats."
- **Age:** "Your age should really not hold you back."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Zach explains how Cal AI grew from influencer-only marketing (~$2M/month) to $5.7M/month by adding performance ads and a creator affiliate program. He covers attribution hacks, ad creative, co-founder roles, hiring, and the speed and self-belief mindset behind the exit.

chunks.heading: Selling Cal AI to MyFitnessPal: the deal and the numbers
chunks.text:
- Zach sold Cal AI to MyFitnessPal (his biggest competitor) at 18, about a year and a half after launch. The two had talked for a while as the relationship built.
- MyFitnessPal bought 100% of the company. Cal AI and MyFitnessPal stay as separate apps. Zach stays through a transition and holds no equity.
- Deal price and cash-versus-stock terms are undisclosed.
- 2025 revenue was $30M. January 2026 revenue was $5.7M, so ARR is now about $50M. A year earlier it was around $1M per month, then over $3M per month.
- His reason for selling: combining resources would help the most people become healthier. The two apps have different core audiences, with overlap where they competed head-to-head.
- Team at sale: about 30 full-time people running app, marketing and design, plus a separate team of virtual assistants.
- He plans to drop out of college, start something new, and says the next one would shoot for a billion.

chunks.heading: Growth channel progression: influencers, then paid ads
chunks.text:
- Stage 1: fitness influencers posting UGC drove growth to roughly $2M/month.
- Saturation: the big fitness influencers share audiences, so each additional one added less. Cal AI then worked with non-fitness influencers, which also worked.
- The big unlock was performance marketing on TikTok, Instagram and Facebook, which took revenue from about $3M/month to $5.7M.
- Influencers still account for "a few million every month" and never died down. Paid ads sit on top of them.
- The mix compounds. Having already been everywhere on social, Cal AI now runs direct-response ads to warmed-up people.
- Organic and influencer awareness make paid ads perform better. Paid ads are where you "liquidate" that awareness.
- Mr. Beast sponsorship:
  - It cost $500K.
  - Zach flew to North Carolina, was in the video, and a friend on the Beast team made the connection.
  - The team never sent an invoice. Zach reached out months later to pay.
  - The ad itself was slightly unprofitable on conversions.
  - The brand authority helped sign more deals later, which likely made it profitable overall.

chunks.heading: Running paid ads: structure, creative and the agency mistake
chunks.text:
- Zach started with an agency to run the influencer content as ads. They capped at about $5K/day in spend. He dislikes agencies because "they're never going to care as much as someone that's actually on the team." He took ads in-house, cycled through a few hires, and built a solid team, which took time and a lot of money.
- Campaign structure:
  - Keep it simple. Over-complicating the many Facebook settings hurts.
  - Cal AI runs mainly one scale campaign (CBO) and one testing campaign.
  - No interest targeting or lookalikes. "The algorithm is just so good at this point that you target with creative."
  - Retargeting is done in the creative itself, e.g. "you've probably seen our ads before."
- Creative is the whole strategy: "You just set it up once and then it's all about the creative." Meta's Andromeda update surfaces ad combinations (ad A then ad B converts), so you need many creatives.
- Optimization event: Cal AI optimizes for starting a free trial (3-day trial, $30/year price).
  - Apple only gives high-quality signal in the first 24 hours, so a purchase 3 days later doesn't reach Facebook in time.
  - The team models whether a given cost per trial start is profitable.
- Retention: Zach says annual health and fitness subscriptions average roughly 30% retention.
- Tools: AppsFlyer as the mobile measurement partner. It never gives fully clear data, so a team member keeps a model of true revenue by source.
- Influencer-style content plateaued as ads at about $10-15K/day. Direct, dedicated videos scaled to about $40K/day. Those say "this is an app I use to track calories, I just take a picture" within the first 5 seconds.
- Many winning creatives have no talking. Examples are gym flexing with music, scanning food, and a caption like how he cut a number of pounds in a month.
- Zach left creative direction to creators through an affiliate program (run on Tribe, coordinated via WhatsApp). Creators make videos exclusively as ads for a percentage of revenue, and some make a lot.

chunks.heading: Attribution tricks for apps
chunks.text:
- App Store custom product pages: create a separate page for paid traffic and link each ad to it. The App Store shows revenue per page, so you see the minimum revenue an ad drove.
  - Inflate by about 30%, since some viewers search the app name themselves.
  - It works well early. It gets hard to manage with many ads.
- Separating influencer from paid revenue: send all paid ads to a custom product page and compare against organic search traffic on the main page.
- Modeling big sponsorships (e.g. the Mr. Beast video):
  - Clicks in the description times a multiplier, assuming maybe 1 in 10 click.
  - Promo code usage, assuming maybe 1 in 8 use codes.
  - The revenue spike on posting day versus an average day.
  - If the methods point to a similar number, treat that as the answer.
- Attribution is "the hardest thing" because of Apple privacy rules. His approach: look at spikes, run incrementality tests (turn a channel off for a few days, then on), and hire gritty people who can separate noise.

chunks.heading: App design built for ads
chunks.text:
- Cal AI has a creator version of the app for filming.
  - It shows a big Cal AI logo on every page.
  - It shows a perfect multi-week streak.
  - Viewers of the recording see the brand name and a flawless-looking app.
- He compares it to burger ads where the burger is sprayed to look perfect.
- Zach knew his marketing strategy from launch: "I always knew from the start, as soon as I launched, what marketing strategies I would take."

chunks.heading: Team, hiring and co-founders
chunks.text:
- Co-founders and roles:
  - Henry Langmack, CTO, met at a coding camp at age 10.
  - Blake Anderson, hands-on advisor who put in early money, advised on influencer marketing and early product design.
  - Jake Castillo, CMO/COO, built the systems to scale influencer marketing and kept things organized.
  - Zach, CEO.
- Early on, founders carried everything. The team used geographic arbitrage with roughly $1K/month developers in India, and he says the work quality showed.
- Investing in real talent changed things. The company started growing on its own, and recent months of his time went to talent, team, vision and hiring.
- When he stepped away for a month at the start of college, morale and numbers stagnated, then recovered when he returned. His takeaway is that someone must set the vision and remind people why they're doing it, which is "extremely important" once you have product-market fit.
- Co-founder advice:
  - Complementary skills matter: an operator, a creative marketer and a technical builder.
  - Friends with the same skill set can build alongside each other rather than on the same product.
  - Define zones of genius and a final decision-maker per area, using the "disagree and commit" approach.

chunks.heading: Starting an app today: ideas, tools and marketing
chunks.text:
- It's "the best time ever to build." Zach points to a high-school friend who built Wrestle AI / Fight AI on Roar, never coded, learned organic TikTok marketing, and now makes about $30K/month.
- Claude Code is the best build tool. Vibe-coding tools are good enough to reach tens of thousands per month, but weaker.
- Don't build unless you know how you'll market it. Solving a problem in your own life usually works.
- Channel strategy:
  - Performance ads (TikTok, Facebook) take a subscription or pay-up-front app the furthest.
  - Another channel may be more profitable at first.
  - Social apps need unique growth strategies.
- With no budget, make videos yourself (maybe 1 in 10 goes viral). Reinvest early revenue into UGC creators, then ads take you from roughly $10K to $100K or $1M to $5M.
- Marketing beats building: "If you had the worst app but amazing marketing, you would still get downloads." Taste and design matter, and the creative person has the advantage over the pure developer.
- To learn paid ads: talk to founder friends and watch free content. Spend roughly $50-100/day on experiments. Learn the 20% that explains 80%, then hire someone who knows the rest.

chunks.heading: Speed, self-belief and mindset
chunks.text:
- Speed was the top core value at Cal AI. He told every new hire on their first call that "speed is our number one core value" and "you should never be the bottleneck." If a call stalled on someone, he got them into the call and had it done immediately.
- Self-belief came from early wins, such as winning a hackathon at 12 against older students. He believes "I can always execute": given a roadmap, he can take it and execute it flawlessly.
- High standards: he kept iterating Cal AI's design until it met the standard he demanded.
- Language: he points to Tony Robbins ("words become thoughts, thoughts become beliefs"). He spoke in "when I'm rich" terms even as a kid, and says to speak of success as already happening.
- Meditation and journaling did not drive his success. He did them before Cal AI, stopped, then started Cal AI.
- Uncertainty: when stuck, he and his co-founders ask what the maximum downside and upside are, make the best decision with what they know, and trust they'll figure it out together.
- His YouTube: raw, unedited rants to document the real founder journey, including that "it still feels like the ship is sinking every day."

chunks.heading: The App Mafia course and lessons on education content
chunks.text:
- Zach and fellow founders lived in a Miami mansion and made content. They launched a paid course, then made it free after about 3 days, and the community add-on earned a few hundred thousand dollars that they spent within a month.
- The larger vision was a "Shopify for apps." It wasn't sustainable because everyone ran other companies and wasn't full-time. Their lives were also at different points.
- Lesson: they deliberately went controversial ("internet money gurus"). He now thinks that was unnecessary.
- He built the course for his younger self, who wanted to start a company but had no idea how.
- College view:
  - He went for the social life and doesn't regret it.
  - He doesn't think college is needed for founders. He'd want a chief innovation officer to keep curricula current, plus Claude Code in classrooms, first-principles problem solving instead of memorization, and AI integrated everywhere.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Zach explains how Cal AI grew from influencer marketing to performance ads and how he ran his first acquisition. He covers playing hard to get, warm intros, expected-value thinking, and how he validates app ideas by treating competitors as proof of demand.

chunks.heading: How Zach sold Cal AI to MyFitnessPal
chunks.text:
Cal AI is a calorie-tracking app where users photograph a meal and AI logs the calories. Zach finished 2025 at $30 million in revenue, and January 2026 alone was $5.7 million. He sold the company to MyFitnessPal, which is owned by private equity. The sale closed in December 2025 and was announced in March 2026. He can't disclose the price. He stays on as Cal AI's CEO for a transition period.

- **May 2025 outreach:** He listed the 10 companies that made the most sense as buyers. He didn't cold-email them. He asked people he knew to make warm intros, framed as "you two should meet" rather than "he wants to sell". Leverage is lost if you're the one cold-outreaching.
- **Result of round one:** Many CEOs shut it down immediately. A few took calls and met the team. Offers came after only a couple of meetings. The first offers were low, about one year of profit.
- **After the lowball:** He politely declined and began to believe Cal AI might just be a cash-flowing business forever. He started looking for a CEO to bring in so he could step away.
- **What changed:** A founder who had sold his company explained how M&A bankers work. They find companies about to go public that want to roll up smaller ones and will pay fair market value.
- **The MyFitnessPal path:** Zach wanted to make Cal AI premium, since long-running big apps all are. He called MyFitnessPal's CEO to ask about freemium. The CEO answered none of it and steered the conversation toward a partnership, which became the acquisition.
- **Posture:** Play hard to get. Show interest, but make clear you're going somewhere either way.
- **Advisors:** He talked constantly to people who had already been through an acquisition. Their deals looked similar to his, so they knew the right things to say.
- **Feelings:** The excitement peaked when the offer came by phone, and the wire itself felt less exciting. He kept the excitement in check until it was signed.
- **Expected value:** His co-founder Blake Anderson taught him EV (chance of winning times the prize) and he used it to decide what to sell for.

chunks.heading: Growth: influencers first, then paid ads
chunks.text:
- **Influencers:** Influencer marketing started the growth and took Cal AI to about $2 million a month.
- **The plateau:** Growth flattened at that level.
- **Performance ads:** Running ads on Instagram, TikTok and Facebook got it over the hump. He says ads now fuel most of the growth.
- **Spend:** Ad spend scaled over time. In January 2026 it was a little over $1 million.

chunks.heading: The MrBeast sponsorship
chunks.text:
- **The deal:** Cal AI paid MrBeast about $500,000 to feature the app in a follow-up video, on his second channel. The video was about whether a contestant kept his weight off after being locked in a gym. Zach knew someone on the team, flew out to the set, and recorded one of the takes about the app himself.
- **Attribution:** Attribution is hard because most viewers go straight to the App Store instead of clicking a link. He used the time overlap with the video, promo code usage and other metrics.
- **Payback:** The estimate was $350,000 to $400,000 from the promo. He calls it a little unprofitable at first, but profitable long term.
- **Why it paid off:** The MrBeast name gave the brand credibility and let him close many more deals afterward. He says the profit from those later deals exceeds the total cost.

chunks.heading: Validating app ideas
chunks.text:
- **Skill to build:** Learning to filter ideas matters more than learning to generate them.
- **Personal fit:** Filtering is personal. He looks for ideas he can market, that could go viral, and that he or people he knows have experienced firsthand.
- **Existing competition:** Competitors already earning revenue are proof, not a deterrent. He saw another calorie app making $200 million a year, which set the minimum ceiling in his mind. "If a company is still growing, that means that there's still a gap."
- **Market sizing:** He mostly trusts his gut instead of formal TAM research.
- **Adjacent comps:** He compares an idea to adjacent companies' revenue to judge how far it could go.
- **Example apps:** He cites Quitter (an app to quit porn, streaks, roadmaps and meditation guides, over $5 million a year) and Claim (class-action lawsuit sign-ups, about $1 million in its first 30 days).

chunks.heading: Mindset and building skills
chunks.text:
- **Self-belief:** He made a video at about 13 or 14 saying he would make a million dollars before graduating high school. He says he shifted his language from "if" to "when".
- **Motivational origin:** He curated his TikTok feed with only motivational speakers like David Goggins. He saw commenters wanting those clips as alarms, and built Grind Clock, a motivational alarm clock app.
- **Skill stacking:** He applies the Pareto principle: learn the 20% that gets 80% of results, enough to hire people smarter than you and manage them. Coding helped him lead a team.
- **Early business:** At 16 he sold his unblocked-games site (5 million users, $60,000 a year from banner ads) for $100,000.

chunks.heading: Money and next steps
chunks.text:
- **Portfolio:** He holds roughly 70-75% in the S&P 500, about 25% in a money market or bonds, and small amounts in Bitcoin and gold. He prefers investing in himself over other people, and plans to move money into his own ventures.
- **Next company:** He will likely raise money for the next venture and keep it more stealthy than Cal AI. He's aiming for a billion-dollar company and wants a hardware component.
- **Idea he tweeted:** A semantic search over your Instagram or X followers, with alerts when someone interesting follows you.
- **AI and the future:** He mentions Steve Cohen's advice to just survive the next three years, since no one knows where AI is heading. He notes humanoid robot hardware is a separate hard problem from AI software.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Zach explains how Cal AI (photo calorie tracker) hit about $20M ARR in 10 months, bootstrapped, through paid influencer marketing. He shares how he validates ideas with an AI wrapper, picks AI app ideas by working backwards from an "aha moment," and why he stayed focused on one app.

chunks.heading: How Zach Yadegari built Cal AI to $2M/month in about 10 months
chunks.text:
- Cal AI is a calorie-tracking app: take a photo of a meal and get calories, protein, fat and carbs. Zach says the scan is about 90% accurate, and notes that FDA nutrition labels can be up to 20% inaccurate.
- He started it at 17 with three co-founders: Henry Langmack (CTO, a friend from a coding camp they attended at age 10), Blake Anderson (found on Twitter, had two earlier apps with a few million downloads) and Jake Castillo (COO, handles organization).
- Launched in May. The first month was slow. The second month did about $30,000. June was the first six-figure month. By October the app did its first $2 million month (about a $24 million annual pace).
- Revenue in the first 12 months would exceed $10 million. The company is fully bootstrapped, has 15 full-time employees, and is profitable at more than 30% margins. The founders pay themselves nothing and reinvest everything.
- Over 95% of subscriptions are annual, so churn data does not exist yet. The app had about 65,000 reviews at 4.8 stars.
- He values the company at roughly $100 million, which puts his stake in the tens of millions on paper.
- Bet behind the product: there is a middle ground between hardcore trackers who weigh every gram and people who track nothing. Cal AI targets that middle.

chunks.heading: Start as an AI wrapper, then build the real product
chunks.text:
- Zach compares the path to dropshipping in ecommerce: the wrapper is the proof of concept, and you manufacture it yourself once you find traction.
- The first version was a thin wrapper over ChatGPT and other AI tools. It had one feature: photo in, calories out, plus a daily breakdown.
- Only after seeing people like it did the team add more features.
- He dismisses the "just an AI wrapper" criticism: "we started as an AI rapper and I think that that's something all apps should do."
- Early validation came from influencer posts, not from family and friends. He discards feedback from family and friends as biased.
- He later pushes the same logic for new ideas: take any existing tool category (calendar, notes, calorie trackers) and ask what the AI version looks like.

chunks.heading: Influencer marketing as the only growth channel
chunks.text:
- All growth came from influencer marketing. Nobody on the team makes videos.
- He says he did make the videos himself for his earlier site, Totally Science.
- Targets are fitness influencers on Instagram and TikTok. Cold outreach mostly goes unanswered; the first response took over two weeks.
- DM format, A/B tested: lead with "paid promo?" because influencers only see the first line or two in their inbox preview. Then: the app lets you track calories just by taking a picture of your food, we think it fits your audience, happy to hop on a quick call.
- Pricing is paid up front, not CPM. CPM would guarantee profitability, but influencers will not accept it because other brands pay in advance.
- This means predicting ROI before any video exists. He looks at the influencer's previous videos and also "not all views are worth the same": read the comment section to gauge how strong their community is, then weigh what to pay. He says they track "a ton of factors and variables."
- Beyond pay, he gives influencers video ideas, using lessons from his earlier TikTok work, but mostly lets them run: "they're the professionals they know what goes viral."
- Start small: the first feedback came from just two influencers posting on their stories.

chunks.heading: Funding it: the unblocked-games site
chunks.text:
- Before Cal AI, in freshman year, he built Totally Science, an unblocked-games website for school laptops. It got around school web filters and was categorized as educational.
- It had a hide key: pressing the Tilde key redirected to Google Classroom if a teacher approached. His dad made him add terms of service banning use during class.
- Growth: about 5 million users via TikTok. Zach recorded his own screen in class and told viewers to go to the site, with a caption "comment what game to add next" to farm comments and push virality.
- Money came from ads on the site. It made about $60,000 over two years, and he sold it for $100,000 at 16. That money funded Cal AI.
- He reinvested nearly all of it into Cal AI; the only thing he spent on himself was a trip for friends to Miami for his 18th birthday.
- Earlier, he taught coding lessons to kids for money from a young age. He says he has coded since age seven.

chunks.heading: Idea frameworks: how he would find the next app
chunks.text:
- **Work backward from the "aha moment."** Find a magic AI trick that works as marketing material, then wrap an app around it so people stay. Cal AI: photo of food, get calories, then tracking and charts keep users. He cites Fitness AI as a parallel (body scanner shows body fat percentage as the hook, workout tracking as the retention).
- **Take an existing popular app category and ask what the AI version is.** Examples he gives: Motion (AI calendar), Turbo Learn AI (record a lecture, get generated notes), AI calorie tracking.
- **Ideas he offers:**
  - An AI journal app that periodically sends insights from your entries, e.g. "on Monday and Tuesday you hung out with Sally and had a bad day." He thinks AI therapists are an open space; existing ones fail to make you feel heard, and voice mode could help.
  - A tool that converts a native iOS app to Android (or the reverse). Cal AI built in Swift for a smoother iPhone experience; the Android port cost tens of thousands of dollars and pulled engineers off iOS, and every feature must be built twice. He thinks AI handles about 90% already, so it could start as an AI-powered agency with human finishing.
  - Remotely configurable onboarding flows with A/B testing. Every consumer app needs an onboarding survey that primes users before the paywall, and changing it currently requires an App Store update that takes days. A system to swap questions and screens remotely and measure conversion, completion and drop-off would be large.
- Good startup ideas often come from papercuts you hit while building. He says working at a startup is a great way to find ideas.

chunks.heading: Focus: why they dropped the app-studio plan
chunks.text:
- For a few months they briefly considered becoming an app studio, building many AI apps and applying the same marketing, because their real edge is marketing, not app development.
