- Equity: a common structure is a roughly 5% pool split among employees, with individual grants such as 0.1% to 0.5%. Cali gave no equity at first, and he says people didn't care and the company underpaid for talent. After equity came, people worked weekends unasked, pitched features and cared about success. He thinks equity is the best tool because it ties people to the whole company, not just one metric.
- Bonuses: tie them to the employee's work. Salespeople on commission are easy to hire, because those who don't produce weed themselves out.
- Every hire should make more than they cost, even though attributing revenue to a role is hard.
- Every employee should have a KPI (one to three metrics) on a dashboard. Missing KPIs repeatedly is a reason to let them go, and crushing them deserves a bonus.
- Pay: he says you can't overpay for real talent. With AI tools, one person can do the work of 10, so one strong hire can be worth several salaries.
- Without aligned incentives, employees do enough to avoid being fired, stay "one foot out the door" and can be poached.
- He strongly prefers in-house employees to agencies. An agency takes on as many clients as possible, does enough to keep them quiet, and its account manager gets little of the upside. You can enforce speed, bias to action and culture on employees, not on agencies.

chunks.heading: Rules for success: speed, action, focus, and doubling down
chunks.text:
- Speed: it was the number one core value at Cali. Don't delay communication. If a teammate needs to weigh in, he adds them to the call on the spot. "The world moves too fast. People will forget about you. Your idea will be taken by a competitor."
- Legal: get the company "somewhat papered correctly early on," but don't spend a day on contracts for a $100 payment. Handshake deals are fine early, since the time and money saved outweigh occasional losses. Get legal after you get rich.
- Sharing ideas: don't hide your idea. A busy successful founder won't steal it, and you lose valuable advice. "Ideas are worthless" and "execution is everything." Many ideas he thought were billion-dollar ideas weren't.
- Bias to action: he has seen companies fail from deliberation and from too many decision makers. He runs "monarchies" where he's the shot caller. Some decisions will be wrong, and the team pivots and fixes them.
- Focus: for an app he reduces everything to three drivers: traffic (downloads), conversion rate (the paywall), and retention leading to LTV. A new feature affects retention, a new channel affects traffic, and a paywall or price change affects conversion.
- Double down: he met a founder whose Facebook ads drove about 90% of the business while the team spent about 90% of its time on other initiatives. His advice was to scale paid ads: better creatives, more spend, a better account structure, and moving in-house from an agency.

chunks.heading: Pricing and A/B testing
chunks.text:
- Pricing method: if competitors exist, start at their price, then A/B test up and down and try different pricing structures. With no competitor, pick something intuitive and test.
- A/B test means showing one price to 50% of users and another to the other 50%, and seeing which makes more money.
- He says nobody can answer "what will perform better" on the spot: "I'm not a computer. No one is." Don't ask people or guess.
- The same applies to paywalls, features, marketing hooks and ad captions. Test video hooks against each other.
- At scale he A/B tests almost every change, because untested changes can quietly hurt the user experience and LTV. Early on, don't let testing slow you down.

chunks.heading: Coming up with and validating ideas
chunks.text:
- Zach says founders' origin stories are mostly "for show." A founder he knows built a billion-dollar custom shampoo company without caring about hair; he just saw a market gap.
- He agrees with Thomas Edison that "ideas are in the air" and free-flowing.
- His approach is to first build the skill of recognizing a good idea. Considerations: size of the market (TAM), the competitive landscape, and any advantages you have. He also uses pattern matching ("this worked in that space, so it should work here"), and he checks whether it solves a problem he has himself.
- Niche problems: if only 1 in 100 people has your problem, that's still about 80 million people out of 8 billion. Don't dismiss an idea because your friends don't relate. Weigh a successful founder's view over friends, who "just want you to play video games with [them] on the weekends."
- Sources of ideas: meeting founders and hearing theirs, problems hit while building another company, and ads for a good idea poorly executed.
- He treats idea generation as a skill, like Jerry Seinfeld writing a joke daily: come up with one new idea a day, since most are bad but quality improves.

chunks.heading: Co-founders, product-market fit, and the mindset for the hard parts
chunks.text:
- Co-founders: pick people with complementary skills (one business/marketing, one product/engineering) and avoid co-CEOs. Set clear ownership, e.g. one owns marketing and the other owns product, so each is accountable.
- Finding them: friends, X, or Y Combinator co-founder matching, which he says is mostly low quality with some diamonds. Don't rush. If it's your idea, vest co-founders with a one-year cliff so you can remove them in the first year with zero equity.
- Product-market fit: he says he has never understood it. His mindset is to build a profitable business from the start and "if you're not profitable, pivot until you are profitable." Sometimes the problem is just the wrong marketing channel, not the idea.
- What makes business hard is the uncertainty, not the steps: random lawsuits, law changes, Apple or Google blocking an app upload, Facebook or TikTok banning ad accounts (both happened to Cali), competitors appearing. Treat every punch as one competitors take too, and keep getting up.
- "You genuinely can't lose unless you give up." He says he hasn't seen anyone keep trying for years and never succeed, and failures teach you until a success takes off.
- Take founder advice with a grain of salt: survivorship and probability apply, and "TikTok ads suck" may be true for one company only. Don't over-optimize either: he worked about 4 hours a day from his bed in Cali's early days, before it hit $1M a month.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Episode 1 of Zach's open-source journey building Flow, a physical alarm-clock dock. He covers picking a big-TAM product, pre-selling during a manufacturing delay, and fixing unit economics with a subscription attach at checkout. The key lesson: spend up to full LTV on acquisition while testing pricing and verifying data.

chunks.heading: Starting Flow with a physical product and a thin cash runway
chunks.text:
Zach started Flow after selling Cal AI. He wanted something physical with a big TAM, and he says "the things with the biggest TAMs are really the things that everyone uses on a day-to-day basis." He also noted that many big companies aren't innovating on technology people use daily.

- He looked at many companies and niches, and found that manufacturing time for hardware is long, which clashes with his software habit ("I have a lot of ADHD. I want things done instantly").
- He landed on a sleep device similar to Brick, which blocks the phone for screen time but has no alarm function. He asked what other use cases a Brick-style device could have, and arrived at an alarm.
- Flow is a bigger brand meant to hold multiple products. The first is the Flow alarm clock: the alarm rings on your phone and you can't stop it until you tap the phone to the Flow dock, so you have to get out of bed.
- Zach says he can't take long breaks from work and got bored fast after selling Cal AI.

chunks.heading: Assembling the team around specific gaps
chunks.text:
Zach picked people for specific roles in the vision.

- **Face of the brand:** he wanted someone charismatic, modeled on the guy who runs Carp's ads (Carp was a brand pumping out content). He met Gabe when Gabe approached him on the street and bombarded him with questions. He checked Gabe's Instagram content, had lunch, and pitched him, knowing he'd be "down for the craziest stuff" with high energy.
- **Website and app builder:** a "grinder" who works quickly and is also strong at product design.
- **Media buyer (Nick):** someone Zach already knew, who runs Meta ads. Zach's view of good media buying: understand the core fundamentals, turn off the extra things Meta tries to turn on for you, and "keep it simple stupid."
- He also works with a designer for the dock and app UI.

chunks.heading: Pre-selling to get past a long manufacturing lead time
chunks.text:
They started in late February by getting the Flow Dock manufactured, calling manufacturers on Alibaba.

- The chosen manufacturer needed 3 months because Chinese New Year was approaching.
- Rather than wait, they launched a pre-sale anyway.
- They made it feel scarce but were clear that orders wouldn't ship for a while: get it now or miss out.
- Side effect: with customers still in pre-sale and not yet holding docks, they couldn't launch a subscription at first.

chunks.heading: Cash discipline: injecting capital and scaling ads to profitability
chunks.text:
A month and a half after launch, the last 30 days were slightly under break-even, and CAC had risen quickly.

- Zach injected $200K at the start, spent $150K, and had $10K left. He spent $7.5K of that paying the ad bill, then injected another $100K.
- His rule for the new money: "We should all be operating under the assumption that like this is all we have." The team had about $105K and needed to achieve profitability off it.
- He scaled ads down despite losing momentum: "sometimes you have to take one step back in order to take two steps forward."
- At a later point, CPAs were $21 against a $29 break-even target (the days before were about $45 and $50), after lowering budgets. They could run about $300K a month profitably but wanted to be "in the millions," which he said would come from raising LTV via subscriptions.
- He notes the uncertainty of tweaking variables: you change something, it hurts, you turn the dial back, but "it's too late and you never get as good as a result that you once had."

chunks.heading: Subscription attach-rate tests and the LTV logic
chunks.text:
Zach and Nick tested a "Flow Plus" subscription offered at checkout with a 3-day free trial.

- First test: opt-in box under the buy button gave about 50% opt-in, which Zach worried was deceptive since it sat below the fold. A bug later turned out to be that the subscription was auto-added to the cart in one test arm.
- Price tests: he cut the initial price from $20 a month to $10 a month to A/B test. Corrected numbers: $40 a year had 77% opt-in versus 45% for $9.99 a month, and the monthly option dropped overall conversion about 30% while $40 a year dropped it only 6%.
- Moving the checkbox above the buy button: attach rates held (about 69% and 63% before, 67% and 69% after), so placement wasn't deception. Overall conversion dipped slightly.
- Retention: free trials tied to a $40 dock purchase mostly converted, because the card is verified by the dock payment. Free trials with no charge see many declines.
- A four-way price split followed: $40 a year, $100 a year, $5 a week, and $10 a month, with a weekly price noted as common in apps but rare in ecommerce.
- Strategy borrowed from Cal AI: don't aim for profit on day one. Get as many subscriptions as possible, break even up front, and make money on the second renewal.

chunks.heading: The unit-economics math that justifies spending more on CAC
chunks.text:
Zach walks through his reasoning for raising the allowable CAC.

- Average order value about $44, fulfillment about $15 per order, leaving about $29 that can be spent to acquire a customer before it's unprofitable.
- Adding the subscription conservatively: $40 a year, at least 50% keeping the box checked ($20), at least 60% of trials converting ($12). That adds $12, taking the allowable spend to about $41.
- His contrast: "An average business person would be like, 'Okay, we have $41... let's still stay under the 41.' A smart business person would recognize that this $41 is a recurring subscription" and would spend right up to that number, making profit from renewals a year later. He calls the numbers super conservative.
- He says it would take one to two months to know monthly renewal rates.

chunks.heading: Doing the work himself and verifying the data
chunks.text:
Zach stays hands-on across product and operations.

- He recoded app UI changes with Codex after redesigning screens in Figma, simplified the alarm-setting flow, and built an AI customer-support dashboard: emails enter a queue, the AI uses guideline documents, responds, and escalates to a human when needed. He also wired up cancel-and-refund for users.
- On coding with AI: "it doesn't feel like coding"; non-technical people "have no excuse" for not building million-dollar apps.
- On email, he notes ramping from zero to thousands of sends needs a warm-up period with Klaviyo and inbox providers.
- He calls customers who abandoned checkout, asking why they didn't buy and whether the subscription option was clear. One said she hadn't looked closely and wasn't sure she could use the product without the subscription.
- He found Triple Whale data inaccurate and that the dock alone, without subscriptions, was losing money. Attach rate on the plans was uncertain, and CAC spiked after adding the subscription to every product.
- Ideas raised: a money-back guarantee if Flow doesn't get you out of bed, and unchecking the subscription by default or making clear in the funnel that the core features work without it. Zach also considered whether Brick, which sells at $60, shows pricing headroom.
- A recurring theme: he thought the subscriptions had it "golden" and found things "way worse than I thought."

chunks.heading: Niche versus winning-product tension
chunks.text: Zach saw an octo-pouch product on Instagram that he is sure would be a winning ecommerce product, since his girlfriend and her friends use it. He had not decided whether to stay in the tight productivity niche under Flow or run ads for any winning product.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Episode 2 of Zach's Flow alarm clock build log. He shows launch pain from a subscription upsell, funnel and price A/B tests, and what he learned from advisors. He ends by dropping a profitable subscription model because customers didn't realize they were being subscribed.

chunks.heading: Launching a subscription alarm product and chasing profitability
chunks.text:
Zach is building Flow, an alarm clock with a dock. The user must physically stand up and tap their phone to the dock to turn off the alarm, and that then blocks their most addictive apps for the start of the day. His goal in this episode is profitability so ads can scale again. His wider target is "$100 million in sales", which he says means selling about 1.3 million units, plus $1 million in a month on a goal he set (34 days to go at the time).

- He launched subscriptions (Flow Plus) a week before the episode, and the early data wasn't good.
- Day-level profit on his new dashboard looked like roughly -$1.5k, then -$300. He first suspected the data was wrong, then found an experiment was the cause.
- That experiment had a variant with no subscription, and that 20% of traffic was "very unprofitable".
- Another 20% got $10 a month, which "was just not making that much money compared to the yearlies". He turned both off.
- That left a three-way split test: $20 a month, $60 a year, $99 a year.
- Refunds were averaging about $1,000 a day, but he reached profitability after setting $99 a year live.

chunks.heading: Fixing confusion about subscription requirements
chunks.text:
Zach found that customers thought they needed the subscription to use the product. He treated this as a product and flow problem, not just a support one.

- Unboxing test: his girlfriend set up Flow for the first time while he watched without helping. She got stuck on the select-sound screen. She hit the back arrow instead of "select sound", so the alarm never set. This is probably why some people think a subscription is needed to set an alarm.
- Planned fix: add a screen that says "your dock is there".
- Customers saw a subscription email, or only noticed the charge after paying, because it wasn't visible in the cart.
- The App Store rating was 3.9. One-star reviews said the subscription was "required". Getting the creators to leave ratings wouldn't fix it long term.
- The Flow Plus code screen wasn't obvious enough. It appears if the app can't match your email to a customer, and he asked for it to be made more obvious.
- Support approach: prioritize customer support and give refunds to anyone who wants one. If someone wants to cancel, they help and process the refund.
- Perspective on rough launches: with Cal AI the first app version was something they were "not proud of". He cites "if you're not embarrassed of what you launch with, you shipped too late", and says the goal is to have all the flows dialed in within four or five months.

chunks.heading: Metrics and internal dashboards
chunks.text:
Zach says the team is "flying an airplane semi-blind" and assigns Alex a complex dashboard in the Flow admin panel.

- He wants metrics for people who purchase: do they download the app right away?
- He wants the number of Flow Plus codes out there and how many have been activated, plus the time to activation, e.g. how many activate within the first day. He flags this as especially important.
- He built an internal profit dashboard called "Triple Whale Shark", modelled on Triple Whale, the real ad-analytics platform many people use. You can click into it to see the formulas behind each calculation, and it serves as a head start for Alex.

chunks.heading: Learnings from a funnel and ad audit
chunks.text:
The team did a two-hour audit and Zach expected "two or three tips" such as one tweak to lower Meta CAC.

- Pricing: test more monthly prices, such as $20 a month. He heard the industry standard is about 25% still subscribed at the end of the year. At $20 a month, LTV would be about $150 for the year, which he says would let them scale.
- Funnel messaging: emphasize "free shipping" and build more social proof.
- Ads: entertaining users works, e.g. Gabe doing stunts, but the messaging needs hammering. He wants claims like "if you wake up after 7:00 a.m., you're 50% less likely to be successful in life".
- Offer testing: try specific odd numbers, e.g. "63% off" instead of "25% off". He wants to read *Influence* by Robert Cialdini.
- A friend said a web funnel (ad to a questionnaire) works well. He built one asking age, gender, phone usage and how often you're late to events, with an interstitial like "X amount of hours a year".
- He recalls Cal AI used about 20 questions, which "reinforce the fact that they have a problem, we have a solution", and had the highest conversion in the ad game. Flow's version: "you're operating at 50% of your potential, if you get it to 80%...".
- Results: going to the funnel before the product page converted about 20% better than going straight to the product page.

chunks.heading: Test results: bundle offer failed, funnel won
chunks.text:
- Test: an offer page led with the two-dock bundle plus free gifts, to raise average order value.
- Result: overall revenue per visitor was down about 5%.
- He notes it works well for some of his other websites (not just supplements), but doesn't know why it didn't work here. Lesson: you have to test it.

chunks.heading: Creative and belief from advisors
chunks.text:
The team flew to North Carolina to meet advisors for a roughly four-hour creative session and filmed an ad with them.

- Biggest value was "just meeting them, just seeing them in person" because it builds belief that "if they can do it, I can do it".
- It showed there is more room to improve creatives, with regular creative meetings and many "micro things".
- Angles to try: ads about the alarm sounds, and ads that start with the alarm ringing and then show all the sounds.
- On the offer, he set $99 a year live straight after the meeting.
- The advisors told them they can do $100 million in the next 12 months, with the only possible bottleneck being shipping.
- After the trip he works through a list of every funnel, ad and offer improvement and sets the web funnel experiment live around 1 a.m.

chunks.heading: Choosing ethics over profit on the subscription
chunks.text:
After $99 a year went live, Zach was profitable, but he got many calls from people who didn't know they were subscribing.

- Lower tiers hid the problem because people cared less; at about $100 a year it became clear.
- A customer was charged $40 for the alarm plus a $99 one-year subscription they didn't intend to select.
- He said they could scale as is with "healthy margins", but "we don't want to run our business this way". It would hurt the brand and is "ethically wrong". He plans many Flow products, and a bad first experience would lose those future customers.
- Decision: switch to a one-time purchase with no subscription model, even though it makes them unprofitable again for now. "Got to do it. This is business."
- Takeaway from one call: a customer was open to paying monthly, so he wonders if more would be.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Zach Yadegari explains how he spotted a pain point in calorie tracking apps, used AI to remove the friction, and went all-in with his co-founders. He covers influencer marketing as Cal AI's core growth engine, reinvesting profits, and the cash-flow lag from Apple's payout schedule.

chunks.heading: Building Cal AI: origin, growth engine and economics
chunks.text: Zach Yadegari is co-founder and CEO of Cal AI, an app where users photograph their food and AI calculates calories and macros. He says it brings in about $1.4 million a month after the app stores' cut. He was 18 when he said this.

chunks.heading: The problem and the AI timing that created the product
chunks.text:
- Zach started working out as a skinny kid. He downloaded one of the most popular calorie trackers at the time and quit 3 days in.
- The reason was friction: the app made him weigh food on a scale and type in everything he ate. He says it was "unsustainable for my lifestyle."
- A year or two later, ChatGPT and other AI technologies launched. He and his co-founders hypothesized they could build an app where "you could just take a picture and AI will do all the work for you."
- They launched and the response was immediately very positive. That told them they had something and they decided to go all in.
- He says the competing apps "are the reason that we started Cali. It's because they suck."

chunks.heading: Going all in: the San Francisco summer
chunks.text:
- With his CTO Henry, he decided to spend the summer doing everything possible to make the app succeed.
- They moved to San Francisco for July, lived in a hacker house and "basically slept in the office."
- He calls that month "the real turning point." They made their first real hires, built up a team and found a rhythm that carried through the next year.
- Cal AI has three co-founders.
- Alongside high school he put in about 40 hours a week on Cal AI, often working during school. Earlier projects had been side projects behind schoolwork; Cal AI was the first he prioritized.

chunks.heading: Influencer marketing is the special sauce
chunks.text:
- He says what Cal AI "really" does is influencer marketing, and "a far majority" of its spending goes there.
- That is the core distribution engine, ahead of any other channel.

chunks.heading: Managing user expectations and refunds
chunks.text:
- Some users expect "X-ray vision," for example that the AI will detect food hidden at the bottom of a bowl. It won't. Every ingredient must be clearly in frame.
- The team teaches correct scanner use early, in the app's tutorial.
- On refunds, Apple processes payments, not Cal AI, so users must request refunds from Apple directly. He calls the belief that the app handles card info a common misconception.

chunks.heading: Cash flow: scaling faster than Apple pays
chunks.text:
- Building the app was cheap because he and Henry programmed it. Money was spent when they launched publicly and scaled.
- Scaling took everything he had made from his earlier site, Totally Science. His co-founder Blake then doubled that amount on top.
- Apple pays about 45 days after a sale. Cal AI was scaling faster than Apple paid, so for months they put money in without seeing a proportional amount come out.
- It took about six months to get ahead of Apple's payout schedule and earn more than they paid out.
- He stresses they were "very profitable" during that period; the gap was a timing problem, not a profitability problem.

chunks.heading: Reinvestment, dividends and founder mindset
chunks.text:
- Most revenue is reinvested into the app. When enough cash is left over, the founders pay themselves dividends. His most recent personal dividend was $100,000.
- He spent much of his earnings, including on a Lamborghini, and says he plans to start saving since he has little else he wants to buy.
- His earlier projects included an unblocked gaming website he built in freshman year of high school, Totally Science, and he started coding at age 7 after begging his mom for a game-making summer camp.
- He rejects age as a self-limiting belief: "When I've wanted to do something, I will just go and do it."
- His goal for Cal AI is to become the biggest calorie tracking app; he considers the job complete when the app is helping people "on autopilot." He plans to build "a generational company" afterward.
- On age: "You're either good or not good at what you do. And then the market will decide the rest."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Zach and the App Mafia crew (Cal AI, Quitter, Umax) explain how they scale hard-paywalled consumer apps: direct-response influencer marketing, occasional big mindshare bets like a $500K MrBeast sponsorship, controversy for reach, a tiny critical path, speed and bootstrapped risk-taking.

chunks.heading: Why Zach started App Mafia and what the course is
chunks.text:
- Zach co-founded App Mafia with Blake, Alex, and Connor. The four were in Vegas for a mobile app convention, then decided to live together in Miami. Zach and Blake had first been thinking about a personal-brand course.
- App Mafia starts with a course on building apps. Zach says they will take backlash because many people think course sellers are bad. His counter is that "for every nine bad courses, there is one that actually provides a lot of value."
- Their differentiator is that everything is public. The apps they built can be verified, and so can the revenue, which he says is "different from pretty much every course seller."
- He says they have seen more than 30 apps doing over $100,000 a month from people who came across their content. Two people he worked with now run companies doing over $1M a month by applying the playbook.
- Their reason for structuring it: they had no incentive to organize the knowledge until they decided to do it together.
- He argues drop shipping, day trading, meme coins, copywriting, and social media marketing are the popular forms of entrepreneurship. These tend to be zero-sum, low-margin, and crowded, and their sellers make money selling courses. App Mafia's pitch is that software is now accessible: AI plus tools like Firebase and Supabase mean you don't need a CS degree or a team of developers.

chunks.heading: Direct response marketing and when to make big brand bets
chunks.text:
- Zach says most of their scaling is direct response, not brand awareness. They know what an influencer post costs and what it returns, and they run it only if it is profitable. The same logic applies to paid ads, UGC, and organic content. Each channel has to be profitable, then they scale the number of posts.
- Cal AI has scaled mostly through influencers and only recently started paid ads (Facebook pay-per-click).
- Recently they have taken bigger swings. They spent $500,000 on a MrBeast video promo, their most expensive ever. By his own view, the view-to-dollar math alone would not have justified it for another influencer.
- His reasons for doing it anyway: second-degree effects. Working with MrBeast makes other brands trust them, people talk about it and share it, and it builds mind share. He says "mind share" gets to a point where you have enough that growth goes hyper, and he doesn't think they are there yet.
- Risk framing at Cal AI: roughly $100,000+ a day in revenue at the time, so $500k is about five days of revenue. Apple payouts are delayed about 45 days, and revenue is not profit, so the real exposure is closer to 15 days of profit. The money was either spent on the video or paid out to themselves, and they decided delaying their own pay was fine.

chunks.heading: Risk tolerance, power-law bets, and bootstrapping
chunks.text:
- Zach's view is that when an opportunity has a clear floor and a large upside, you take it every time. The team's framing for the MrBeast spend: they expected at least about $300,000 back from the $500k, with upside in the millions.
- The earlier example was Alex Eubank. They spent $100,000 a month on a deal when Cal AI was at about $500k a month in revenue. Within a few months it was over $2M a month, which they credit largely to him and the influencers he helped them get. Zach says it took them a while to learn to take these opportunities every time.
- Quitter: Alex built an app, and Zach pitched an idea to help men quit porn. They started with Reddit and X marketing. Zach put $3,000 into influencers and, paying 20% up front on deals, leveraged it into about $15,000 of placements with religious creators. That got Quitter to about $1,000 a day. He says it could have failed and he trusted his gut.
- On cheap, small bets in the same spirit: a 20k deal with a large Christian creator (Bryce Crawford) was justified by Zach even if only $10-15k came back, because of word of mouth, easier access to more creators, and larger later deals. Their biggest competitor markets only through churches, so it targets that audience on the social media channels they are good at.
- Bootstrapping downside: every dollar comes out of your pocket, so it is harder to place huge bets than with VC money. Zach says his team would "yolo everything" into a play they believed in.
- Worst-case thinking: if everything burned, they could rebuild in a month or two, so he treats flights or small outlays as non-risks.
- He says the VC path shouldn't be the default. Raising money carries an implicit expectation of chasing a huge outcome, and bootstrapping lets you work on progressively harder things as a stepping stone, like Elon (Zip2, PayPal before Tesla/SpaceX).

chunks.heading: Controversy, social capital, and algorithmic reach
chunks.text:
- Zach argues people are too scared of controversy. His view is that cult-like followings come from having a core of fans and a core of haters, and that people who change how things are done are the ones remembered.
- Their approach: they built apps by seeding the algorithm on TikTok and Instagram. For App Mafia, they plan to sacrifice some social capital (dropping a course) for controversy and then use YouTube vlogs of their lives.
- On hiring: the more algorithmic reach you have, the higher-quality talent you attract. He uses Cluely and Roy Lee as examples. Inbound from sharp, hardworking people is a payoff of posting publicly.
- Longer-term content plan: systems built so that their lifestyles are the content, with a team filming and them helping on ideation.
- Brand idea for Quitter: move from direct response to seeding the algorithm so the culture shifts (porn becomes uncool, Quitter becomes cool), taking a cue from products that turned into movements like Whoop and Strava.

chunks.heading: Team, hiring, speed, and prioritization
chunks.text:
- Cal AI has 30+ employees; about half are virtual assistants and the rest are specialized roles. Zach says people assume it's a solo founder, which is not true.
- His view on solo "one-person billion-dollar company" talk, based on Blake's experience: hiring a full-time employee made output jump immediately. Find cracked people and get out of their way (the Richard Branson idea).
- Hiring advice: the founders can all code, design, and market well enough to judge quality. He notes people with no technical knowledge keep hiring poor engineers because they can't tell the difference.
- Reducing cognitive load: a private chef saves hours and improves energy, which helps the business.
- Prioritize the core: for consumer apps with hard paywalls, three things matter: getting people to download, converting downloads, and getting them to stay (marketing, conversion, retention). Spend roughly 80% of time there and 20% on the rest, and let small fires burn.
- Speed is a core principle at Cal AI, Quitter, and App Mafia: if something is not done quickly you "slowly fall behind" and don't hit escape velocity. Their approach was to set deadlines after early weeks in Miami drifted.
- They killed a launch video that cost about $25-35k because it wasn't good enough, and made another. His rule: if it isn't much better than anything they've done, kill it regardless of cost.
- Confidence and many decisions build intuition. Taking life less seriously, shipping, and accepting embarrassment gives more data.

chunks.heading: Goals, advice, and mindset
chunks.text:
- Zach set a goal at 14 to make a million dollars before graduating high school (there is a YouTube video of it). He did, but said it didn't feel like a finish line and that goals should keep shifting. He thinks lacking goals to chase is where depression comes from.
- He kept a 4.0 GPA in high school while building Cal AI and argues people have time (average screen time is hours a day).
- Advice that nothing is universal: for every story of what worked, there is a counterexample. He says only the laws of physics are universal, so lean into your own attributes.
- Companies on the brink of death sometimes survive and sometimes die for reasons beyond their decisions, so survivorship stories overstate what "it takes."
- Hardest thing he's overcome: being jumped at a party (broke his nose, needed surgery) while the team was taking acquisition calls, which he describes as the hardest week or two of his life.
- Future plans: no near-term need to build a billion-dollar company, preferring to enjoy being young; the team could do it but wants to be YouTubers for a while. He mentions long-term interest in AI hardware like a Whoop competitor with local inference, and AR/glasses software.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Zach Yadegari explains how Cal AI paid MrBeast $500K for a sponsorship that roughly broke even short-term and paid off through credibility. He also covers using expected value to decide on selling a company, validating ideas against proven adjacent apps, and surviving an uncertain AI future.

chunks.heading: Using Mr. Beast sponsorship as a growth and credibility play
chunks.text:
- Zach and Cal AI paid MrBeast "half a million dollars" to be placed in one of his videos. It was a follow-up on his second channel, on whether a contestant kept the weight off after being locked in a gym for 100+ days.
- A contact on MrBeast's team helped Zach get the sponsorship. Zach was flown out to watch it happen and filmed one take himself talking about the app, which the video used.
- Attribution is imprecise because most viewers go straight to the App Store instead of clicking a link. Zach estimated results from time overlap, promo code usage and a few other metrics.
- On those estimates, the $500,000 spend brought back roughly $350,000 to $400,000 directly, so it was "a little bit unprofitable" right away.
- He believes it was profitable long term, or will be. Being able to say the app was in a MrBeast video gave Cal AI "way more credibility" and let it do many more deals afterward.
- The profit from those follow-on deals has exceeded the total amount spent on the MrBeast placement.
- At the time, the Cal AI team was about 30 people, a bit more than that.

chunks.heading: Making decisions with expected value (EV)
chunks.text:
- Zach learned decision frameworks from his co-founder Blake Anderson, who taught him EV and related principles.
- EV is the chance of winning times the prize. Compare a certain outcome against the chance of losing it all against the possible upside, and generally pick whichever is greater.
- He used EV to think through selling the company. He asked what the chance was of getting to a given outcome, what the chance was of it falling apart, and what the sale was worth against those.
- Worked example (from the discussion, which Zach confirmed was "a perfect example"): a $100 sure offer has an EV of $100. Holding out for $500 at a 10% chance is worth $50, so taking the offer wins. You also have to factor in ongoing risk the business falls apart if you keep running it.
- The point is an objective way to decide instead of acting on emotion, mood, fear or greed.

chunks.heading: Validating startup ideas instead of just generating them
chunks.text:
- Zach says coming up with ideas is a skill, but the more important skill is a framework for filtering good ideas from bad ones, so you can sift through them quickly.
- He says the framework should differ per person, because it depends on your skill set. His own filter is ideas that are good for him: things he's interested in and thinks he could "kill" and blow up.
- He looks for ideas that are very marketable and can go super viral.
- He looks for problems he has experienced firsthand, or that people he knows are experiencing, so he knows exactly who he's building for.
- He benchmarks against adjacent companies. For Cal AI he saw another app making $200 million a year, which set "the lowest floor of what we could get to."
- Before you have that intuition, you can analyze TAM, the competitive landscape and a few other objective metrics. Zach himself mostly goes by gut on TAM and didn't research the calorie-tracking TAM before starting Cal AI.

chunks.heading: Competition as proof the market works
chunks.text:
- Zach says many people are deterred when they see that someone else already built their idea. He thinks they shouldn't be.
- Existing growing competitors are proof the idea works. If a company is still growing, there is still a gap and people who are underserved.
- Markets can be big enough for many apps to succeed. He noted that at his entrepreneurship class, everyone pitching responded with "that already exists" and was discouraged by it.

chunks.heading: Why apps are a good starting point, and app ideas he points to
chunks.text:
- For someone starting out, with one of their first projects and aiming for a reasonable goal like a million-dollar company or a few million dollars, Zach thinks apps are a great space right now. This is true especially with AI, but also without it.
- Quitter, built by a friend, helps guys quit porn. It doesn't really use AI. It gamifies the process with a streak, a roadmap, rewards and meditation guides, and it now makes over $5 million a year.
- Claim (spelled "CLAIM") lets people sign up for class action settlements, such as a Pepsi suit, to get $10 to $15 when it settles. Zach says it made about a million dollars in its first 30 days, but was taken off the App Store.
- Zach says an easy "few million dollar idea" is semantic search over your Instagram or X followers. It would let you find, for example, entrepreneurs or people you'd want to date among your followers, and alert you when someone interesting follows you. He tweeted about it and it blew up.
- For his own next company he says he's "shooting for like a billion dollar company," so smaller million-dollar app ideas aren't worth his time now. He plans to be stealthier about the next one than he was with Cal AI.

chunks.heading: Staying consumer-focused and hedging against AI uncertainty
chunks.text:
- Zach says he loves building products for consumers. Hearing that someone loves something he built is the biggest compliment. He wants to keep doing that and would like a future company with a hardware component, possibly alongside software.
- On AI, he says he sees a world possibly changing completely soon if AI labs reach their goals. That is scary but exciting.
- He relayed advice from Steve Cohen at a dinner: don't try to predict the end state. Work out how to extend your companies' timelines about 3 years and survive the intermediate period, then figure out what's next.
- He argues people overweight software when thinking about AGI. Humanoid robots and hardware are a separate problem that may be just as hard, and companies like Physical Intelligence are working on it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Zach Yadegari explains how self-belief and "when, not if" language pushed him toward a teenage revenue goal, and why learning the 20% that matters lets you hire and manage smarter people. He also walks through selling his app company: a lowball first round, a mindset reset, warm intros, and leaning on founders who had sold before.

chunks.heading: Self-belief and the "when, not if" mindset
chunks.text:
- Zach built self-belief by wanting the outcome so badly he "needed it to be true." As a young teen he filmed a kitchen video saying he would make a million dollars before graduating high school, and he always believed in his heart he would do it.
- He deliberately shifted his language from "if" to "when." As a kid he told his mom "if I'm rich when I'm older," then corrected himself to "when I'm rich."
- He still had doubts ("can I actually do this?"), but he keeps self-belief as the thing that got him past obstacles like "I have to go to college / get a degree first."
- In the year before he started Cal AI, he curated his TikTok For You page to show only motivational speakers (his feed was "David Goggins yelling at me"). He still consumes motivational content, just less than before.

chunks.heading: Finding app ideas by watching what commenters ask for
chunks.text:
- His first app, Grind Clock, was a motivational alarm clock where users pick a motivational speaker's voice as their alarm sound.
- The idea came from watching those motivational TikToks: commenters kept saying the clip pumped them up and asking how to make it their alarm, and there was no easy way to do it.
- Test he used: he wanted it for himself, and the comment sections showed clear unmet demand from others.

chunks.heading: Skill stacking over being a genius
chunks.text:
- Zach agrees that you don't need to be a prodigy. Being good enough at building plus strong at marketing and entrepreneurship is the valuable combination.
- Coding is getting easier with AI tools, and his coding ability mainly helped him learn to lead a team.
- He applies the Pareto principle: learn the 20% that gets 80% of the results. That is enough to hire people smarter than you and manage them well.
- He did this across multiple areas, which let him build strong people around him and put systems in place.

chunks.heading: Running an M&A process for his first sale (Cal AI)
chunks.text:
- Timeline: the process began in May 2025, a few months before college, because he wanted a normal freshman experience without running a company. The sale closed in December, was announced in March 2026, and the wire hit the same day it closed.
- He ran it like a sales cycle: he listed the 10 companies that made the most sense as buyers.
- Warm intros over cold outreach: he had been told you lose leverage by cold outreaching, so he had people he knew introduce him, framed as a cool company worth meeting rather than him asking.
- Several CEOs shut it down right away, some even saying "cool company, not interested." A few took calls and met the team, and offers came quickly after a couple of meetings.
- Timing: he and the buyers avoided influencing anything during peak season (January and February), which is part of why the announcement waited.
- Being undervalued: he felt Cal AI was extremely undervalued relative to the first offers.

chunks.heading: What happened after the low first offers
chunks.text:
- The first offers were roughly one year of profit, less than the company would make in a year. He politely turned them down.
- He then wondered whether the company was simply unsellable and began accepting it might be a cash-flowing business forever. He started looking for a CEO to bring on so he could step away.
- The turning point: another founder who had sold told him how M&A bankers work. They build lists of companies you've never heard of, including ones about to go public that want to roll up smaller companies and will pay fair market value.
- He agrees with the pattern that the second round of interest comes when you care less and the company is stronger because you committed to building it to last.
- He frames this as the "no one's coming to save us" moment, which strengthened his resolve.

chunks.heading: Making Cal AI premium and how the real deal started
chunks.text:
- While committed to building a lasting business, he reasoned that any big, decade-old app he could think of was premium, so he began working toward making Cal AI premium.
- He tried to get free guidance from the MyFitnessPal CEO, who is strong at freemium, framing the call as catching up. The CEO answered none of his freemium questions, which Zach says makes sense since it wasn't in their interest.
- Instead, that conversation pivoted to a possible partnership, and that is how the actual acquisition talks began.

chunks.heading: Negotiating advice for first-time sellers
chunks.text:
- Play a little hard to get, a push and pull. Show interest without seeming too interested, and signal that you're going places regardless of whether they get on board.
- Find advisors who have been through acquisitions and keep them on the phone throughout the process. He did this constantly. Acquisitions across companies look similar, so they told him the right things to say as situations came up.
- It was his first time and the buyer was owned by private equity, so they were seasoned pros, which made experienced advisors more valuable.
- He felt the excitement when the offer first came by phone, but made himself quell it until anything was signed, and it never felt as good again afterward.

chunks.heading: The Lamborghini course rage-bait launch
chunks.text:
- He lived in a Miami house with entrepreneur friends. The original plan was to build companies side by side and share learnings, then record content, which required paying videographers and editors.
- To at least break even, they launched a course on making apps. He says they are "business people at heart," so they wanted it to cover its costs.
- They deliberately chose a controversial, Andrew Tate-style angle: "sell the dream, sell the lifestyle instead of sell the product." Videos featured a Lamborghini and money in the air. He says it was intentional rage bait and not a real representation of their characters.
- It took over the Twitter timeline but started beefs that weren't great. His assessment: it makes the story more interesting, but he would take a different angle next time.
- Launching on Twitter was also a mistake in targeting, since Twitter users weren't the audience the course was meant for. It was just their native platform.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Zach reflects after Cal AI's best month (over $3M in May), explaining that the biggest growth bottleneck is public skepticism about accuracy. He lays out how he plans to counter it with influencer scripts, honest messaging and educating users on features beyond the viral scan, and what he would do differently on future projects.

chunks.heading: Cal AI's accuracy perception as the growth bottleneck
chunks.text:
- Zach says May was Cal AI's best month ever, over $3 million in revenue.
- Early in the month he had $160,000 revenue days, driven mainly by appearances on Fox News, TMZ and other live national platforms.
- Later in the month revenue settled to roughly $80k a day on average. He expected it to fall back toward $100k a day, not hold the spike.
- After analyzing recent social posts, he concludes the biggest bottleneck is that many people still don't believe Cali is accurate.
- Those people think the app is only a scanner. In fact it also has a food database (track food like on MyFitnessPal) and barcode scanning.
- He describes it as the company versus many influencers making attack videos plus a comment community. Comments like "finally someone's coming out and saying this" get thousands of likes (he cites one with 5,000).
- His main goal at that point is to push the narrative that Cali is accurate.

chunks.heading: Market saturation and the share of customers lost to skepticism
chunks.text:
Zach gives rough estimates, not measured numbers:
- Almost 100% of the fitness niche has heard of Cali.
- Some portion of that niche is potential customers. He guesses maybe 25% (up to about 50%) of potential customers have started the app.
- There is still room to grow.
- He believes at least 50% of potential customers won't give the app a chance because of the "not accurate" claims.
- He gives skeptics some credit: the scanning claim is hard to believe.
- Marketing mostly shows the scan feature because that is what goes viral. As a result most people don't know the database and barcode features exist.

chunks.heading: The lesson: pre-empt the credibility objection early
chunks.text:
- His biggest takeaway for future projects: he should have handled the accuracy objection earlier.
- If, from the start of Cali, they had published material on why it's accurate while scaling, "that would have actually helped a lot."
- By now it is "kind of out of hand" and "going to be a big uphill battle."
- General rule he draws: when the viral hook creates an obvious skepticism, answer it in your own content before it hardens into community consensus.

chunks.heading: Tactics being considered to fix the narrative
chunks.text:
- Have influencers talk to camera about accuracy, then "spark ad" (promote) those videos to put engagement behind them.
- Make high-quality videos in-house and post them. His concern is that these may not reach the skeptical audience that influencers' followers represent.
- Short influencer videos first, then longer videos that break everything down.
- Plan: start with the short version, assess how people take it, then double down.
- He is writing influencer scripts himself, going through the attack videos and their comments, which he finds overwhelming because there are so many points to rebut.
- He frames it as a step back to take two steps forward, sometimes necessary, while still pursuing other initiatives and going broader.

chunks.heading: The influencer script he wrote (accuracy messaging)
chunks.text:
Key points of the script:

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Starter Story spends a day with the Cal AI founders in New York. Zach Yadegari explains why they went all in, how four friends with separate domains and deep trust made hard decisions, and why solving your own problem makes product and marketing click.

chunks.heading: Building Cali AI with a four-person founder team
chunks.text:
- Zach's co-founders each owned a domain and trusted the others to run theirs. He says that's why they "didn't really have any fights": everyone was "so focused on the one thing that we became experts in."
- Roles at Cali AI: Zach was CEO, Blake Anderson was co-founder/investor/advisor, Jake Castillo was CMO/COO (marketing and operations), and Henry was CTO.
- Zach met Henry at a coding camp at age 10, and the friendship turned into daily gaming and shared projects.
- Zach DM'd Blake to meet him. As Cali ramped up, the team needed a COO, and Zach recruited Jake, whose work at StudyBody he knew.
- When the founders met, Zach says they decided to "burn all the boats" and go all in on Cali, because they now had "the dream team."
- The team was still working for a salary on another app when Cali began. It was hard to believe it would be the app that let them go self-employed.

chunks.heading: Cali AI revenue trajectory
chunks.text:
- Zach was 19 at the time of the interview. He started coding at 7, put his first app on the App Store at 12, and started a company in his freshman year of high school.
- That earlier company reached 5 million users over 2 years and made about $60K a year. He sold it at 16.
- Cali AI made $30K in its first month and over $100K in its second month.
- Within 8 months it reached $1M a month.
- At the time of the interview, Zach put it on track for roughly $50-60M for the year.
- Cali AI was later sold for multiple millions of dollars. The exact price was not disclosed.

chunks.heading: Choosing not to sell early, and how trust settled it
chunks.text:
- At the end of 2024, the team received low eight-figure acquisition offers.
- The team was conflicted. The money was life-changing, but they cared deeply about the product and saw a lot of growth left.
- They resolved it through constant open communication. They called each other all the time during that period.
- Through that trust they reached a collective decision not to sell then.
- Zach's view: without trust between co-founders, "you're not going to take your company to its true ceiling and its true potential."

chunks.heading: Finding ideas and marketing by solving your own problem
chunks.text:
- Zach says building something that solves your own problem makes everything fall into place.
- You know what you'd want from the product, so the design becomes intuitive.
- You know who you're marketing to because you're marketing to yourself, so you know the pain points to hit.
- If you don't have an idea, he suggests looking for something that would actually help you.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Zach Yadegari explains how Cal AI, a bootstrapped photo calorie tracker, scaled to a $35M run rate and 20-30K daily downloads within a year of launch. Covers retainer-based influencer marketing, onboarding and paywall A/B testing with Superwall, a viral founder brand, and hiring specialized talent from X.

chunks.heading: Cal AI's first year: $35M run rate, 20-30K daily downloads, 250 influencers on retainer
chunks.text:
Zach describes Cal AI in May 2025, about a year after launch. The app tracks calories from a photo of your food. He says it is only possible now because of AI breakthroughs, but "mainly because of APIs like ChatGPT. We did not train our own model to do this."

- First line of code was written around March 2024, and the app launched in May 2024.
- It reached its first $1M in sales on September 4, 2024, about five months in.
- In May 2025 Zach said the annual run rate was "over 35,000,000", assuming no growth.
- He said revenue collected in 2025 was "a little over 10" million (he first said about 9 million, then corrected himself).
- The app gets "20 to 30,000 new downloads" every day.
- The company is bootstrapped, with no outside funding (stated in the page's summary, not in his words).
- He expected 25 to 50% of annual subscribers to renew in year two. Cal AI had no data yet because it had just passed its first anniversary.

chunks.heading: Influencer marketing on monthly retainers is the biggest channel
chunks.text:
Influencers on TikTok and Instagram are Cal AI's biggest channel. The reasons for that, per Zach:

- About 250 influencers are on monthly retainer, each integrating Cal AI into their content.
- Zach says the largest earns "tens of thousands per month" for four posts.
- Total influencer spend the previous month was "mid six figures".
- Pricing starts from the creator's account metrics. The team looks at views and engagement, because "not all views are valued the same". It then sets a minimum and maximum it is willing to pay.
- Creators get no script. "They are the professionals. They know what goes viral for their audience." Cal AI's job is making sure they integrate the product well.
- He prefers commission-only pay ("that would be the dream"). The reality is that creators want guaranteed payment, and "if we're not gonna do it, another brand will."
- Doubling down on influencers was the main focus of the last twelve months, and new creators are signed every month.
- Of the 17 staff, about half work on marketing and influencer management.

chunks.heading: The company was meant to be an app studio, but Cal AI absorbed all the attention
chunks.text:
- The founders saw their influencer strategy as the thing other app builders lacked. The plan was to apply it to several apps under a holding company.
- By the time the other app ideas finished development, Cal AI was growing so fast that "it deserved all of our attention."

chunks.heading: Onboarding: add questions, add reassurance screens, animate them, test each change
chunks.text:
The onboarding flow was built through A/B testing.

- **Start:** no animations or GIFs. It was bland and asked only the questions needed to compute daily calorie intake.
- **Added questions:** he added questions that don't affect the result, such as which diet the user follows. Conversion rose. His hypothesis, which he says other people see too, is that the user invests more time.
- **Reassurance screens:** a "thank you for trusting us" screen and a "you're gonna lose weight faster with Cal AI" screen both lifted conversion.
- **Animation:** animating those screens lifted conversion again. He sums it up as "a game of creating hypotheses and then testing them out."
- **Sign-in at the end:** moving sign-in to the end of the flow was "the biggest by far" improvement, because of the drop-off at that step. Zach confirmed asking for sign-up at the end was intentional.

chunks.heading: Paywall and trial: Superwall, high conversion, and heavy testing
chunks.text:
- Paywalls are built in Superwall. Zach says conversion is "much higher" with it and it "has allowed us to run so many tests."
- He says the team lacks feature testing but runs "so many tests" on paywalls.
- There is a three-day free trial. He says 20 to 25% of new users convert, either to paying right away or into the trial.
- Testing for the rest of the product is custom-coded and uses Mixpanel. Zach says it only started around January, "three months ago", and "we are behind on that front and have mainly operated through intuition." Now every new feature is tested.

chunks.heading: App Store optimization: stuff keywords into the name and subtitle, use intuition first
chunks.text:
- The team fits in "as many keywords as we can" in the app name and subtitle.
- It used no keyword tools such as AppFigures. Early keywords came from what the founders, as power users, would search for.
- Later it talked to agencies for more input, but "most of that is just what our intuition told us."

chunks.heading: Speed, specialized hiring, and recruiting from X
chunks.text:
- Zach says speed is Cal AI's number one core value: "push things out fast, develop it fast, push it out fast, see the test results quickly." He thinks most companies move too slowly.
- Hiring is the top priority, but for specialized talent. Examples he gives: one person whose only job is paywall experiments, one who only makes the food scanner more accurate, and one who only owns the homepage.
- Most of the talent came from X. A user redesigned a Cal AI screen and the team is now interviewing him. Zach also posted looking for a Facebook ad buyer.
- Headcount was 17 for several months and was heading to about 22 within a month or two. Everyone is remote.
- No agentic automation yet. The team is all humans, and some developers use Cursor.

chunks.heading: A viral founder brand turned into TV appearances
chunks.text:
- Zach's X post about his college admissions got 28 million views. His personal statement post got 40 million views on its own. He expected two or three million.
- He says he is "wired to know when posts will go viral" from growing up on social media.
- TV stations reached out, one or two at first and then more as he appeared. He calls it a snowball effect: other stations get FOMO and see that he "can present well on camera."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Superwall case study on how Cal AI ran 123 paywall experiments across 46 trigger points and grew monthly revenue 3x+ in 10 months. Zach's own contribution is one quote: treat paywalls like the product, ship fast, measure, iterate. The rest is Superwall and agency commentary.

chunks.heading: Paywall experimentation as a compounding growth system
chunks.text:
Zach treats the paywall like any other product surface: "We treat paywalls the same way we treat the product — ship something, measure it, and improve it tomorrow." He argues that spending weeks debating what a paywall should look like means you've already lost: "Just test it."

- Cal AI joined Superwall in March 2024, shortly before public launch. It started with one onboarding paywall and a few price points.
- Hard-coded paywall changes, App Store review waits and one-variant-at-a-time learning would have throttled the team. They needed experimentation cheap enough to run constantly across pricing, design, messaging and placement.
- Over about two years the team ran 123 A/B experiments on iOS, 160 unique paywall designs, 424 total variants and 46 trigger points. That is roughly five real experiments per month.
- 61 of those experiments were on the onboarding paywall, testing layouts, offer framing, pricing presentation, urgency treatments and creative direction against live traffic.
- Zach's takeaway: speed beats perfect theory. Ship, measure and iterate fast enough to learn from real users.

chunks.heading: Results of the paywall program
chunks.text:
- Monthly revenue grew more than 3x in 10 months.
- Trial-to-paid conversion improved 31% (relative) over 12 months.
- 87% of new users see a paywall.
- 57% of paywall viewers start a transaction.
- 63% of started transactions complete.
- During the January New Year's resolution surge, installs nearly doubled month-over-month. The heavily tested funnel was ready, which he frames as compound interest on over a hundred small optimizations paying off at the right moment.
- Cal AI's growth curve: $28K in month 1, $115K in month 2, $1M monthly recurring revenue within 6 months, and 15M+ downloads and roughly $40M annual revenue within 18 months.
- The case study credits distribution through short-form video and creator-led acquisition for demand, but says installs alone don't create a subscription business. The conversion system did.

chunks.heading: Monetize every high-intent moment, not just onboarding
chunks.text:
Cal AI built 46 trigger points instead of relying on a single onboarding paywall. The lesson is a much larger testing surface: more chances to learn and more places to improve revenue.

- **Onboarding:** the first high-intent purchase moment for new users.
- **Transaction abandon:** exit-intent recovery flows when users back out of checkout.
- **Freemium feature gates:** camera scan, barcode scan, label scan, macros, analytics, progress photos and health score.
- **Win-back flows:** separate messaging for expired trials, lapsed subscriptions and reactivation campaigns.
- **Lifecycle messaging:** paywalls tied to push notifications and email journeys.
- **Upsells:** family plans, lifetime deals, body scan reports and nutrition chat add-ons.

chunks.heading: Treat the paywall as a creative surface
chunks.text:
Cal AI tested formats that felt like product experiences rather than static purchase screens.

- **Spin-wheel paywall:** users "unlock" a discount by spinning a wheel. This turns a standard purchase decision into a more dynamic moment. The team kept iterating on discount framing, urgency, animation and how aggressively the offer was positioned.
- **Video paywalls** were also tested.
- Messaging, motion and visual framing can change how a product pitch feels.

chunks.heading: Test price architecture, billing cadence and checkout together
chunks.text:
Performance is rarely driven by one variable, so Cal AI tested combinations rather than debating them in the abstract.

- The matrix of active price points expanded broadly: weekly, monthly, quarterly, annual and lifetime combinations were all part of the test surface.
- Creative, price architecture, billing cadence, trial structure and checkout destination all interact.
- They added web checkout via Stripe. Giving users more than one way to pay opened another revenue channel and reduced unnecessary checkout friction compared with only the default App Store flow.

chunks.heading: Never settle on a winner
chunks.text:
- Per the case study, the team found a winning variant and immediately started testing against it. That relentlessness is why numbers kept compounding month after month.
- Zach's operating principle is "small weekly improvements compound into outsized revenue growth when the team keeps shipping and measuring."
- Even losing experiments are treated as learning about what users respond to.
- His advice for subscription apps: start with your first experiment, and the compounding takes care of the rest.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Zach Yadegari explains at TechCrunch Disrupt how Cal AI grew virally by recruiting and paying many small influencers. He spotted early signal when one post drove about a thousand users in two days, then scaled by negotiating performance-based payouts with creators who have tight communities.

chunks.heading: How Zach found his influencer growth loop
chunks.text:
- Cal AI launched in 2024 as an AI-fueled calorie tracking app. Zach built it into a company that generated over $30 million in revenue in two years, and MyFitnessPal acquired it in March (2026) for an undisclosed amount.
- His main growth strategy was deploying "a small army of influencers" to promote the brand.
- The first signal came when a single influencer's post about Cal AI drove roughly a thousand new users over two days.
- He treated that as proof the channel could work: "we figured out, okay, this can actually work for us, and so we started recruiting influencers as fast as we could — paying as many people as possible to start posting for us."

chunks.heading: Why paid influencer posting scaled predictably
chunks.text:
- Zach describes the result as "a clear formula": "It was pretty linear, but it was extremely fast."
- "Linear" means each post reaches a certain number of viewers, and a consistent share of those viewers converts to users.
- Because output per post was predictable, adding more influencers produced a proportional increase in installs, so growth became a matter of recruiting and paying more creators.

chunks.heading: How Zach structured influencer deals
chunks.text:
- He negotiated rates with influencers, promising a specific payout tied to a specific scale of reach.
- Many influencers are "broke college kids" who "just want cash," so straightforward cash deals work.
- The pitch to the creator is: "we'll pay you this, but we need to get us at least this amount of use[rs] and keep posting until you get there."
- The influencer's obligation is to keep posting until the agreed audience or reach target is met, not just to publish one post.

chunks.heading: Choosing influencers whose reach can be measured
chunks.text:
- The "biggest thing" for Zach was finding influencers with "very tight communities."
- The key criterion is that an influencer's reach can be quantified, which makes the pay-for-reach agreements and the linear conversion math workable.

chunks.heading: Other views Zach shared at TechCrunch Disrupt
chunks.text:
- He credits his family with giving him the freedom to pursue his ambitions.
- On college, he said "the only real reason to go to college is if you want to have a fun social time as a kid and be with other people."
- His new startup, Persona, is an AI agent company that raised $10 million. Its stated mission is to "make computing seamless with human life."
- Persona's assistant is meant to "live anyplace with internet connection," including "iMessage, app, email, phone call," and Zach plans to build a "hardware ecosystem around" the app.

chunks.text: Fortune profile of Zach Yadegari (18), who built the Cal AI calorie-tracking app to roughly $30M a year. Covers building from a personal pain point, TikTok and influencer-led growth, selling an earlier site for $100K, and why he still goes to college while rejecting the standard path.

chunks.heading: Starting out: apps as a teenager
chunks.text:
- Zach started coding at 7, gave coding lessons at $30 an hour by age 10, and put his first app, "Speed Soccer", on the App Store at 12.
- In high school he built "Totally Science", a site where classmates could play unblocked games at school. It grew to 5 million users over two years and made $60,000 a month from banner ads he placed on the site, six figures in total.
- He sold it at 16 for $100,000. He says "that's when I started building apps". Everything he built up to that point was free.
- He calls the early apps "small projects". Cal AI is the one that took off.

chunks.heading: Finding the idea: solve your own annoyance
chunks.text:
- Cal AI came from his own fitness journey. He was very skinny his whole life and wanted to bulk up. He found most of the progress came from diet, so he tracked calories and ate in a surplus.
- The most popular calorie app at the time was "an awful experience". He couldn't eat in the cafeteria with friends because he was eating pre-portioned meals weighed on scales, and he skipped restaurants because he couldn't know the calories.
- He argues that wasn't sustainable for a kid in school. It was bad enough that he gave up on much of his fitness journey for a while.
- He had basic coding skills and saw the rise of AI tools like ChatGPT and Claude, so he decided to build the app himself: take a picture of your food and get the calories.

chunks.heading: Team and launch
chunks.text:
- He brought the idea to people he knew he could trust: a friend from coding camp and two people he met on X. The co-founders (Henry Langmack, Blake Anderson, Jake Castillo) were all older than him.
- They launched Cal AI in May 2024.
- Early growth came from TikToks and influencer partnerships: "We started making TikToks, we started partnering with influencers, and then we had pretty explosive growth."
- The positive feedback encouraged him. In July 2024 he moved to San Francisco with his co-founders to focus and hired about 15 employees.

chunks.heading: Growth, pricing and funding
chunks.text:
- Roughly a year and four months after launch, Cal AI brings in about $30 million annually. Fortune reviewed financial records showing several million dollars of revenue per month. The team is over 30 people.
- The app is free to download on the App Store and Google Play, with subscriptions at $2.49 per month or $29.99 per year.
- He says the app has a 90% accuracy rate.
- Investors constantly tried to "throw money at us", and the team turned it down.

chunks.heading: Views on college and the standard path
chunks.text:
- He rejects the formula that everyone should follow: "get good grades, go to a good college, get a degree, get a job, and then start making money". He says he hated that notion and used to fight with his parents about it.
- He was widely rejected by Ivy League schools despite a 4.0 GPA, a 34 ACT and entrepreneurial success. He went to the University of Miami anyway.
- He frames it as lifestyle, not career: "I look at it as I'm paying $100,000 a year for a vacation."
- He is undeclared, dropped out of the business school, and now takes philosophy classes. He keeps one entrepreneurship class but says he's "not gaining much from the class material".

chunks.heading: Building a community: App Mafia
chunks.text:
- In Miami he lives in a house with other app-building friends aged 18 to 26, all successful entrepreneurs.
- They are building "App Mafia", a community and brand that educates people online with content on how to build apps.
- His stated aim: "We're basically trying to lead the forefront of Gen Z builders."
